summary: Yāmuna's defence of the Vedic authority of the Pāñcarātra. Contrasting it with the 'Māheśvara' tantras, he names four Śaiva groups - Kāpālikas, Kālāmukhas, Pāśupatas and Śaivas - and reports the Kāpālika six insignia and yoni-meditation, the Kālāmukha skull and corpse-ash practices, the Pāśupata five categories, and the claim that initiation makes one a brahmin at once; he judges all of them outside the Veda.

alt_summary: Yāmuna's treatise establishing the validity (prāmāṇya) of the Pāñcarātra: it sets out the objections — that the Pāñcarātra is outside the Veda, that its followers (Sātvatas/Bhāgavatas) are a low temple-serving caste, that Bādarāyaṇa refuted it — and answers that it was spoken by the omniscient Lord, is Vedic in root, and that its followers are brahmins; it distinguishes it from the Śaiva schools (Kāpālika, Kālāmukha, Pāśupata, Śaiva).

summary: A short tantra in two recensions praising the Akulavīra — the one reality beyond all distinctions, the same in everything, beyond mind, caste, ritual, fasting and pilgrimage. title: Amaraughaśāsana
summary: A prose treatise ascribed to Gorakṣanātha, printed in the Kashmir Series with a commentary. It sets out the elements, breaths, channels, ten doors and seven bonds of the body, locates the 'desire, poison and spotless' (kāma, viṣa, nirañjana) at the root of the brahma-staff, rejects rival definitions of liberation (cutting off karma, Veda-recitation, the supportless, meditation on form, bindu and nāda, Kaula union, the movement of kuṇḍalinī) and defines liberation as the mind seeing the mind in sahaja-samādhi.

The chapter colophons call it an Upaniṣad, a knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) and a treatise on yoga (yogaśāstra).
attribution.scholarly: An integral part of the Bhīṣmaparvan whose unity and date are debated; many scholars see a single composition drawing on Upaniṣadic, Sāṃkhya-Yoga and Bhāgavata materials, others posit layers.

The Kashmir recension (commented on by Abhinavagupta and Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha) has additional verses and many variant readings. A verse found in some manuscripts (the 'Gītāmāna') speaks of 745 verses (620 by Kṛṣṇa, 57 by Arjuna, 67 by Sañjaya, 1 by Dhṛtarāṣṭra); it is not in the Critical Edition.

title: Brahma Sūtra

structure.description: 4 adhyāyas × 4 pādas. Śaṅkara's recension: 555 sūtras (pāda counts 31, 32, 43, 28 | 37, 45, 53, 22 | 27, 41, 66, 52 | 19, 21, 16, 22). Other schools divide and number differently: Rāmānuja 545 sūtras, Madhva 564; Nimbārka 549 and Vallabha 554 (these two counts low confidence). Adhikaraṇa counts also differ (Śaṅkara c. 191–192; Rāmānuja c. 156; Madhva c. 223 — low confidence).

editions.name: numerous Devanāgarī editions with Śaṅkara's bhāṣya (e.g. Nirṇaya Sāgara)

notes: Pāda themes (per Śaṅkara): 1.1 texts with clear marks of Brahman; 1.2 unclear marks, Brahman as object of meditation; 1.3 unclear marks, Brahman as object of knowledge; 1.4 doubtful words (avyakta, ajā) claimed by Sāṃkhya; 2.1 objections from smṛti (Sāṃkhya, Yoga) and reason answered; 2.2 critique of Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Buddhists, Jains, Pāśupatas and (per Śaṅkara) Pāñcarātra; 2.3 creation of the elements and nature of the jīva; 2.4 the prāṇas; 3.1 transmigration (for dispassion); 3.2 the states of the self and the nature of Brahman; 3.3 combination of meditations; 3.4 auxiliaries of knowledge and the āśramas; 4.1 repetition and the effects of knowledge; 4.2 departure at death; 4.3 the path of the gods; 4.4 the liberated state. All sūtra numbers in this shard follow Śaṅkara's numbering.
summary: Bādarāyaṇa's aphorisms systematizing the Upaniṣads in four adhyāyas — samanvaya (all Upaniṣadic texts converge on Brahman), avirodha (no conflict with smṛti, reason or rival systems, which are critiqued in 2.2), sādhana (transmigration, the states of the self, the meditations, the auxiliaries of knowledge) and phala (repetition of meditation, the knower's freedom from karma, departure, the path of the gods, the liberated state). Every Vedānta school is founded on a commentary on it.

title: Brahmasūtrabhāṣya of Bhāskara (Bhāskarabhāṣya)
summary: Bhāskara's commentary on the Brahma Sūtras: Brahman really transforms into the world through its power; souls are parts of Brahman distinguished by real adjuncts (aupādhika bhedābheda); liberation comes after death through knowledge combined with lifelong ritual duty; it attacks Śaṅkara's doctrine of māyā as Mahāyāna Buddhist in origin.

structure.description: four adhyāyas, each of four pādas, following the sūtras

scholarly.text: c. 8th–9th c. CE (after Śaṅkara, before Vācaspati who answers him)

summary: one of the thirty-seven works of Madhva collected as the Sarvamūla ('root of all'); Madhva's concise commentary on Bādarāyaṇa's Brahmasūtras, reading them as establishing Viṣṇu, full of qualities and free of defects, as the Brahman they inquire into, and as teaching difference, gradation of souls and liberation by grace won through knowledge. It supports its readings with many quotations from Vedic, Pañcarātra and Purāṇic sources.
notes: Opening verse and 1.1.1–1.1.2, 3.1.8, 4.2.16–17, 4.3.10–15, 4.4.19 checked against the Devanāgarī e-text in sources_raw/raw_etexts/vedAntam/dvaitam (github.com/sanskrit/raw_etexts); numbering follows that copy and may differ in other editions.

notes: Sub-commentaries: Padmapāda's Pañcapādikā (→ Prakāśātman's Vivaraṇa), Vācaspati's Bhāmatī (→ Amalānanda's Kalpataru → Appayya's Parimala), Ānandagiri's Nyāyanirṇaya, Govindānanda's Ratnaprabhā.
summary: Śaṅkara's commentary on the Brahma Sūtras, opening with the 'adhyāsa-bhāṣya' on superimposition as the root of all empirical dealings; it reads the sūtras as teaching the non-dual Brahman, the unreality of the world apart from Brahman, knowledge alone as the means to liberation, and liberation while living, and it critiques Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, the Buddhist schools, the Jains, the Pāśupatas and the Pāñcarātra.

summary: Śaunaka asks Pippalāda; teaches prāṇa as the self, the four seats of the person (navel, heart, throat, head) with waking, dream, deep sleep and the fourth, and — in its second part — that the true topknot and sacred thread are knowledge, so the knower who renounces wears the 'thread' of the Self and the ekadaṇḍin's sandhyā is meditation.

title: Brahmacārin Sūkta (Atharvaveda 11.5)
summary: The hymn of the Vedic student: the brahmacārin moves quickening both worlds; the teacher, initiating him, holds him three nights as an embryo; with fuel, girdle, toil and tapas he fills the worlds; by brahmacarya and tapas the king protects the realm, a maiden wins a husband, the gods struck down death.

title: Brahmajñānāvalīmālā

attribution.tradition: Śaṅkara
attribution.scholarly: attribution to Śaṅkara doubted or rejected by most modern scholars (style, doctrine, citations); probably by later Advaitins of the Śaṅkara tradition

summary: A short verse garland of Brahman-knowledge whose most quoted verse states the 'drum-beat of Vedānta': Brahman is real, the world is false, the jīva is Brahman alone and not other.

title: Brāhmaṇa Gītā

attribution.tradition: Kṛṣṇa relates a dialogue between a brāhmaṇa and his wife (and other embedded dialogues) to Arjuna
attribution.scholarly: part of the Anugītā

tradition.text: composed by Vyāsa; the war and teaching at the junction of the Dvāpara and Kali ages

scholarly.text: within the Mahābhārata's growth c. 4th c. BCE - 4th c. CE; the Śāntiparvan's Mokṣadharma belongs to the later layers

summary: A brāhmaṇa teaches his wife the inner sacrifice of the senses and breaths and the knowledge of the Self beyond them; part of the Anugītā (owned by unit U05).

title: Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa

attribution.tradition: Proclaimed by Vāyu ('vāyuprokta' in the colophons), the eighteenth Purāṇa, 12,000 verses; the Lalitopākhyāna is its appended Uttarabhāga told by Hayagrīva to Agastya.
attribution.scholarly: Shares its core with the Vāyu Purāṇa; the Lalitopākhyāna is a much later Śākta/Śrīvidyā addition; the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa also claims a Brahmāṇḍa origin.

tradition.text: Vyāsa, end of Dvāpara

scholarly.text: core c. 4th-6th c. CE; Lalitopākhyāna much later

structure.description: four pādas (Prakriyā, Anuṣaṅga, Upodghāta, Upasaṃhāra) in three bhāgas; the 12,000-verse saṃhitā ends at Uttarabhāga ch. 4; Lalitopākhyāna = Uttarabhāga chs. 5-44

notes: chapter checked in the GRETIL e-text of the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa (Venkateshwara ed.)
summary: A classic Purāṇa of creation, cosmography, time, manvantaras and dynasties (with śrāddha and Paraśurāma narratives), closing with the dissolution and the city of Śiva, to which the Lalitopākhyāna is appended.

title: Brahmasiddhi

structure.description: 4 kāṇḍas: Brahma, Tarka, Niyoga, Siddhi

notes: Commentaries: Vācaspati's Tattvasamīkṣā (lost), Citsukha's Abhiprāyaprakāśikā, Ānandapūrṇa's Bhāvaśuddhi, Śaṅkhapāṇi's vyākhyā (last three low confidence).
summary: Maṇḍana Miśra's independent Advaita treatise in four chapters (Brahma-, Tarka-, Niyoga-, Siddhi-kāṇḍa): Brahman as bliss and consciousness; avidyā residing in the individual selves as non-apprehension and misapprehension; perception grasps being, not difference; critique of the view that the Upaniṣads enjoin (niyoga); liberation through knowledge made direct by repeated contemplation (prasaṅkhyāna), with works as helpful.

title: Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa

attribution.tradition: Told by Sāvarṇi to Nārada about the Rathantara-kalpa (per the lists); 18,000 verses.
attribution.scholarly: The extant text is a late Bengal recasting centred on Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in Goloka; it differs from the text summarised in older lists.

tradition.text: Vyāsa, end of Dvāpara

scholarly.text: extant form c. 15th-16th c. CE, Bengal (older core lost)

structure.description: four khaṇḍas: Brahma, Prakṛti, Gaṇapati, Kṛṣṇajanma

summary: Kṛṣṇa as the supreme Person in Goloka with Rādhā as his śakti; Prakṛti's five principal forms (Durgā, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Sāvitrī, Rādhā); Gaṇeśa's birth; Kṛṣṇa's life with a strong Rādhā-centred devotion.

title: Brahmavidyā Upaniṣad

canon.group_scheme: editorial grouping of the 108 used by the Adyar Library series and most modern catalogues; the Muktikā itself lists the 108 by Veda only

attribution.tradition: Śruti: revealed, without human author (apauruṣeya); the Muktikā presents it as one of the 108 Upaniṣads that Rāma teaches Hanumān, each belonging to a Vedic śākhā
attribution.scholarly: anonymous; assigned to a Veda by the Muktikā list, not by any surviving śākhā transmission

tradition.text: Śruti: eternal and authorless; no human date

scholarly.text: Scholarly accounts differ by text. Several Yoga Upaniṣads (e.g. Amṛtabindu, Amṛtanāda, Kṣurikā, Tejobindu, Nādabindu, Dhyānabindu, Brahmavidyā, Yogatattva, Yogaśikhā, Haṃsa) survive in shorter northern versions that are older; the expanded southern recensions (as in this collection) borrow from medieval haṭha works and were probably compiled in South India, perhaps as late as the 18th c. (Bouy 1994).

summary: Oṃ's body and measures; the jīva's natural repetition of haṃsa; haṃsa-vidyā as the only means; the guru as Hari; three kinds of teacher; sakala and niṣkala; piercing the three knots; ends in an 'I am' litany.

title: Brahmayāmala (Picumata)

scholarly.text: Nepalese manuscript dated 1052 CE; text perhaps 7th–8th c.

structure.description: about 12,000 verses in some 100 paṭalas (approximate; not verified)

editions.name: S. Hatley, The Brahmayāmalatantra or Picumata, vol. I, IFP/EFEO/Hamburg 2018
Cs. Kiss, The Brahmayāmalatantra or Picumata, vol. II, IFP/EFEO/Hamburg 2015
Muktabodha e-text M00319

notes: Contains Kāpālika and sexual rites; summarised only.
summary: The chief early Yāmala tantra of the Vidyāpīṭha, teaching the cult of Kapālīśabhairava and Caṇḍā Kāpālinī with yoginīs, Kāpālika observances and powers; first in the Śrīkaṇṭhīya's Yāmala group, and the source ('Picu') of the Maṅgala group's Bhairavī.

title: Bṛhad-Vaiṣṇavatoṣaṇī
summary: Sanātana's commentary on the tenth canto of the Bhāgavata (abridged by Jīva as the Laghutoṣaṇī).

title: Bhartṛprapañca's commentary on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (lost)
summary: A pre-Śaṅkara commentary teaching that Brahman is both one and many and that liberation needs knowledge combined with works; known only from reports and refutations in Śaṅkara's Bṛhadāraṇyaka commentary, Sureśvara's Vārttika and Ānandagiri's glosses.

attribution.tradition: Bhartṛprapañca (identified by Ānandagiri as the opponent in Śaṅkara's commentary)
attribution.scholarly: fragments collected by M. Hiriyanna (1924)

scholarly.text: before Śaṅkara (c. 6th–7th c. CE or earlier)

notes: All knowledge of this work comes from opponents (reported_by_opponent). A commentary on the Kaṭha Upaniṣad is also reported (low confidence).

title: Bṛhadāraṇyaka-bhāṣya-bhāvabodha
summary: Raghūttama Tīrtha's commentary (Bhāvabodha) on Madhva's Bṛhadāraṇyaka-bhāṣya; Raghūttama is called Bhāvabodhācārya after his Bhāvabodha commentaries.
notes: The Bhāvabodha is in the raw_etexts corpus; its attribution to Raghūttama is from memory.

title: Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārttika
summary: Sureśvara's massive verse sub-commentary on Śaṅkara's Bṛhadāraṇyaka commentary; source of the semblance theory (ābhāsa-vāda) of the jīva, of the principle that any method (prakriyā) that leads to knowledge of the inner self is valid, and of a detailed refutation of Bhartṛprapañca.

title: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad
location_in_parent: final part of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (Mādhyandina 14.4-9; also closing the Kāṇva recension, src:satapatha-brahmana-kanva)

attribution.tradition: śruti, 'seen' by the sages whose teaching it records; not a human composition
attribution.scholarly: anonymous compilation within the Vedic schools (śākhās), incorporating older materials

tradition.text: Revealed scripture (śruti): in the Mīmāṃsā and Vedānta view without human author and beginningless; the texts themselves trace their teaching through lineages of teachers back to Brahma/Prajāpati and brahman, the self-existent

scholarly.text: c. 7th-6th c. BCE (rough estimate; widely held to be pre-Buddhist)

structure.description: 6 adhyayas, 47 brahmanas (Kāṇva recension, used for refs here: adhyaya.brahmana.kandika); in three kandas: Madhu-kanda (1-2), Yājñavalkya- or Muni-kanda (3-4), Khila-kanda (5-6)

summary: The largest and probably oldest Upanisad: the cosmic horse; the self that was alone in the beginning and said 'I am'; 'I am brahman'; Ajātaśatru's teaching of the sleeping person; the two forms of brahman and neti neti; Yājñavalkya's dialogues with Maitreyī, with the brahmins at Janaka's court (Gārgī, Uddalaka, Śākalya) and with Janaka on light, dream, sleep, death and karma; da da da; the contest of the breaths; the five fires and the two paths; lineages of teachers.

editions.name: Sanskrit text with Śaṅkara's bhasya (Advaita-Sarada e-text; GitHub sanskrit/raw_etexts mirror)
editions.licence: public domain text; e-text licence per repository

F. Max Muller, The Upanishads, SBE 1 and 15 (1879, 1884)
P. Olivelle, The Early Upaniṣads (1998; text and translation)

notes: Veda affiliation: White Yajurveda (Kāṇva and Mādhyandina recensions)

title: Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya (Madhva)

attribution.tradition: Madhva (Ānandatīrtha), counted among his thirty-seven works
attribution.scholarly: accepted as Madhva's

tradition.text: composed by Madhva (Ānandatīrtha); the tradition dates his life to 1199–1278 or 1238–1317

summary: one of the thirty-seven works of Madhva collected as the Sarvamūla ('root of all'); Madhva's commentary on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, reading it as teaching Viṣṇu's supremacy and his difference from souls and matter, often by etymological explanation of names and by quotations from other scriptures.

title: Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣya of Śaṅkara
summary: Śaṅkara's longest Upaniṣad commentary; it expounds the self as pure consciousness known through neti neti, the renunciation of the knower and of the seeker, and it refutes Bhartṛprapañca's combination of knowledge and works.

title: Bṛhadbhāgavatāmṛta
summary: Sanātana Gosvāmī's narrative theology with his own commentary Digdarśinī: part 1, Nārada's search for the greatest recipient of Kṛṣṇa's grace, rising to the gopīs; part 2, the cowherd Gopakumāra's journey through the worlds to Goloka.

structure.description: two parts, each of seven chapters

title: Bṛhaddevatā
summary: Śaunaka's metrical treatise on the deities of the Ṛgveda hymns, hymn by hymn, with the legends (itihāsa) behind them; it lists the women seers (brahmavādinī) of the Ṛgveda and discusses how the one Ātman is praised under many deities.

attribution.tradition: Śaunaka
attribution.scholarly: late Vedic–early classical compilation; date debated

alt_summary: A verse treatise on the deities addressed in the Ṛgveda hymns, with the stories (itihāsa) told to explain them and a discussion of how the deities are ultimately one power in three stations.

structure.description: 8 adhyāyas in ślokas

title: Bṛhaddharma Purāṇa

attribution.tradition: An Upapurāṇa.
attribution.scholarly: A Bengal Upapurāṇa, important for Bengali caste and ritual history.

summary: Dharma, Gaṅgā-māhātmya, the Goddess and the ordering of castes in Bengal.

title: Bṛhajjābāla Upaniṣad

attribution.scholarly: anonymous; assigned to a Veda by the Muktikā list, not by any surviving śākhā transmission

scholarly.text: Sectarian Śaiva Upaniṣads are generally placed by scholars in the medieval period, with wide uncertainty; a few (e.g. Atharvaśiras, Kaivalya) are usually thought older than the rest.

summary: Bhusuṇḍa asks Kālāgnirudra about sacred ash: its origin from Sadāśiva's five faces, its five names (vibhūti, bhasita, bhasma, kṣāra, rakṣā) and their meanings, preparation, ash-bath and tripuṇḍra, and the merit and liberation it confers.

title: Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa

attribution.tradition: An Upapurāṇa of Nārada.
attribution.scholarly: Distinguished by scholars from the Nāradīya Mahāpurāṇa; strongly Vaiṣṇava, with the praise of the name 'harer nāma'.

notes: The verse 'harer nāma harer nāma harer nāmaiva kevalam / kalau nāsty eva nāsty eva nāsty eva gatir anyathā' is attributed to the Bṛhannāradīya by Gauḍīya authors; location not checked.
summary: Vaiṣṇava devotion and the power of Hari's name in the Kali age.

title: Bṛhaspatismṛti
summary: A lost legal smṛti, reconstructed from quotations in the digests; its treatment of legal procedure and the titles of law was highly regarded.

title: Bṛhatī

editions.name: Bṛhatī with Ṛjuvimalā, ebhāratī-sampat digital text (ends in adhyāya 6: 'etāvaty eva mātṛkā')

summary: Prabhākara's commentary on Śabara's bhāṣya, the root text of the Prābhākara school; transmitted with Śālikanātha's Ṛjuvimalā. The available text breaks off in the sixth adhyāya.

title: Bṛhaṭṭīkā (lost)
notes: Its scope (a longer treatment of the tarkapāda?) and which later quotations derive from it are uncertain; verses on omniscience quoted in Buddhist and Jain works are sometimes assigned to it.
summary: A lost larger work of Kumārila, known through later quotations and references.

title: Caitanya Bhāgavata
summary: Vṛndāvana Dāsa's Bengali biography of Caitanya (originally titled Caitanya Maṅgala), rich on the Navadvīpa period, the nocturnal kīrtanas and Nityānanda; in three khaṇḍas (Ādi, Madhya, Antya).

structure.description: Ādi, Madhya and Antya khaṇḍas

title: Caitanyacandrodaya
summary: Kavikarṇapūra's ten-act Sanskrit drama on Caitanya's life (1572 CE per tradition).

title: Caitanya Caritāmṛta
summary: Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja's Bengali verse biography and theology of Caitanya, interspersed with Sanskrit verses, in three parts: Ādi (17 chapters), Madhya (25) and Antya (20). It sets out who Caitanya is (Kṛṣṇa with Rādhā's mood), his teachings to Rūpa, Sanātana, Rāmānanda, Sārvabhauma and Prakāśānanda, and his last years of divine madness at Purī.

structure.description: 3 līlās: Ādi 17, Madhya 25, Antya 20 chapters (cited here as 1.x.y, 2.x.y, 3.x.y)

scholarly.text: completed c. 1612–1615 CE (one colophon reading gives 1615; an alternative reading 1581)

title: Caitanya Maṅgala (of Jayānanda)
summary: Jayānanda's Bengali biography of Caitanya, notable for an account of his death.

title: Caitanya Maṅgala (of Locana Dāsa)
summary: Locana Dāsa's Bengali song-biography of Caitanya, based on Murāri Gupta.

title: Caitanya Upaniṣad
summary: A text presented as part of the Atharvaveda that describes Caitanya as the Lord's appearance in Kali; published with a commentary by Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura in the late 19th c.

tradition.text: Part of the Atharvaveda

scholarly.text: Late; first attested in 19th-c. Gauḍīya publication

title: Camakam (Camaka-praśna)
summary: The Yajurveda litany that follows the Śatarudrīya: a long series of petitions 'and … for me' (… ca me) — food and impulse, the breaths, mind, speech, eye and ear, strength and life, truth and faith, well-being, the Vedic rites and their implements, and finally the numbers — each to be made fit by the sacrifice (yajñena kalpantām).
notes: Recited with the Śatarudrīya (Namakam-Camakam); ritually the formulas accompany the 'stream of wealth' (vasordhārā) offering of the agnicayana (moderate confidence).

title: Caṇḍamāruta
summary: Doḍḍayācārya's commentary on Deśika's Śatadūṣaṇī, continuing the polemic against Advaita.

title: Cāndra-vyākaraṇa
summary: Candragomin's grammar, closely based on Pāṇini but without Vedic rules and accents, transmitted especially in Buddhist circles (Nepal, Tibet, Sri Lanka).

title: Candrajñānāgama

attribution.tradition: revealed by Sadāśiva from the upper (Īśāna) face; first received by Ananta, then Bṛhaspati (Kāmika pūrva 1.30–92; Kiraṇa vidyāpāda 10)
attribution.scholarly: texts now transmitted under this title are mostly South Indian redactions centred on temple ritual; their relation to the early scripture of the same name is not established here

structure.description: Rudrabheda no. 19 in the Kāmika's order; 14 upabhedas in the Kāmika's list

editions.name: Muktabodha M00263, M00273 (the latter describes itself as a pratiṣṭhātantra); Vīraśaiva recension M00201

notes: Kiraṇa 10.16/10.23: 'Candrabhāsa' of Ananta → the gods' priest (Bṛhaspati). Śrīkaṇṭhīya: 'Candrāṃśu'. In the Kāmika's image of the scriptures as Sadāśiva's body it is the chest (pūrva 1.93–101). Lists checked by the Phase-B author against local e-texts: Kāmika pūrva 1.30–92 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/Kamikagama.md (Kāmika Pūrvabhāga, Madras 1909 Grantha ed. as transcribed)), Kiraṇa vidyāpāda 10.3–27 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/kiranagama.md (Kiraṇa vidyāpāda, South Indian printed text as transcribed)) and the Śrīkaṇṭhīya list quoted by Jayaratha on TĀ 1.18 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/tantrAlokaH_viveka-vyAkhyA-sahitaH-1.md (Tantrāloka with Jayaratha's Viveka, KSTS vol. 1)).
summary: No. 19 of the 28 Śaiva Siddhānta mūlāgamas (Rudrabheda). According to the Kāmika it was first received by Ananta, then Bṛhaspati. The Kāmika assigns it 14 upabheda(s): Sthira, Sthāṇu, Mahānta, Vāruṇa, Nandikeśvara, Ekapādapurāṇa, Śaṅkara, Nīlarudraka, Śivabhadra, Kalpabheda, Śrīmukha, Śivaśāsana, Śivaśekhara, Devyāmata. A 'Candrajñāna' also appears in the Vāmakeśvara's list of 64 tantras.

title: Candrajñānāgama (Vīraśaiva recension)
summary: The Vīraśaiva recension of the Candrajñāna Āgama (kriyā- and caryā-pāda), one of the Āgamas the tradition reads as teaching Vīraśaiva dharma in its later portion.

editions.name: Muktabodha digital library e-text M00201

notes: Distinct from the Śaiva Siddhānta transmission of the Candrajñāna (U08).

title: Candrāvalokana
summary: A short dialogue in which Maheśvara instructs Matsyendra on the śāmbhavī seal (inner aim, outer unwinking gaze), the dissolution of breath and mind, the 'new-moon, first-day and full-moon' of the eyes, desire (kāma), poison (viṣa) and the spotless (nirañjana), the mind as the seed from which bindu arises, and the six centres.

editions.name: Muktabodha e-text M00506 ('Candrāvalocakana')

notes: Several verses are shared with the Haṭhapradīpikā (e.g. the verse ending 'dambha-mithyā-pralāpaḥ' = HYP 4.114). Date unknown.

title: Candrikāprakāśa

tradition.text: Rāghavendra entered his brindāvana at Mantrālaya in 1671

summary: Rāghavendra Tīrtha's commentary on Vyāsatīrtha's Tātparyacandrikā.

title: Caṅkaṟpa Nirākaraṇam
summary: Umāpati's refutation of nine views close to the Siddhānta — Māyāvāda, Aikyavāda, Pāṣāṇavāda, Bhedavāda, Śivasamavāda, Saṅkrāntavāda, Īśvarāvikāravāda, Nimittakāraṇapariṇāmavāda and Śivādvaita — especially on the relation of the freed soul to Śiva.
notes: The list of nine is given at moderate confidence.

title: Caraṇavyūha
summary: A short treatise listing the branches (śākhās, caraṇas) of the four Vedas and their extent — e.g. the five Ṛgveda śākhās (Śākala, Bāṣkala, Āśvalāyana, Śāṅkhāyana, Māṇḍūkāyana) — ascribed to Śaunaka or Kātyāyana; the Atharvaveda has its own Caraṇavyūha among its Pariśiṣṭas.

attribution.tradition: Śaunaka (or Kātyāyana)
attribution.scholarly: late compilation; its counts of śākhās are traditional

title: Catuḥślokī (of Vallabha)

editions.name: Acintyaviśvasādākhya (Muktabodha M00272) — relation to the Cintya not established here

notes: Kiraṇa 10.4/10.8: 'Acintya' to Dīpta; Dīptarudra → Gopati → Ambikā. Śrīkaṇṭhīya: 'Cintya'. In the Kāmika's image of the scriptures as Sadāśiva's body it is the toes (pūrva 1.93–101). Lists checked by the Phase-B author against local e-texts: Kāmika pūrva 1.30–92 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/Kamikagama.md (Kāmika Pūrvabhāga, Madras 1909 Grantha ed. as transcribed)), Kiraṇa vidyāpāda 10.3–27 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/kiranagama.md (Kiraṇa vidyāpāda, South Indian printed text as transcribed)) and the Śrīkaṇṭhīya list quoted by Jayaratha on TĀ 1.18 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/tantrAlokaH_viveka-vyAkhyA-sahitaH-1.md (Tantrāloka with Jayaratha's Viveka, KSTS vol. 1)).

notes: Recited with ancillary texts (aṅgas): Kavaca, Argalā, Kīlaka before, and the three Rahasyas (Prādhānika, Vaikṛtika, Mūrti) after; the naming of the three caritas' deities as Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī and Mahāsarasvatī comes from the dhyāna verses and the Rahasyas, not from the 13 chapters themselves. summary: The Goddess, Mahāmāyā, is the eternal source and power of the world who deludes even the wise and grants liberation; she wakes Viṣṇu to slay Madhu and Kaiṭabha, arises from the gods' combined radiance to slay Mahiṣa, and as Ambikā with Kālī/Cāmuṇḍā and the Mothers slays Śumbha, Niśumbha and their generals; hymned as present in all beings ('yā devī sarvabhūteṣu'), she promises to return whenever demons oppress the world.

summary: A Vaiṣṇava encyclopedia best known for its Pretakalpa: the process of dying, Yama's messengers, the thumb-sized person, the year-long road to Yama's city past sixteen towns and the Vaitaraṇī river, judgment, the preta state and its signs, and the rites that give the dead a body and join them to the ancestors.

title: Garuḍa Purāṇa, Pretakalpa

attribution.tradition: Kṛṣṇa's answers to Garuḍa's questions on the fate of the dead (with a Bhīṣma-Yudhiṣṭhira dialogue in ch. 22).
attribution.scholarly: A manual of death and the rites for the dead; recensions differ in chapter count (35 in some editions).

structure.description: 49 chapters (Venkateshwara)

notes: Chapter topics (from the colophons of the local e-text): 1 questions; 2 after-death rites and karmic results; 3 hells; 4 cremation, deaths in pañcaka; 5 annual rites and the road to Yama; 6 vṛṣotsarga; 7 five pretas; 8 self-śrāddha; 11 the openings of departure; 12 only dharma follows the dead; 14 gifts; 15 Yama's world; 16 the preta's journey; 19 entry into Yama's hall and new bodies; 20-23 the abode, harassment, dreams and signs of pretas and their release; 24-25 untimely deaths and children; 26 sapiṇḍana; 27 Babhruvāhana and the preta; 32 embryology; 36 death by fasting; 38 higher worlds and liberation; 39 impurity periods; 44 bad deaths; 45 annual śrāddha; 46-48 destinies and karma; 49 means of liberation. verse number checked in the GRETIL/Sansknet e-text of the Garuḍa Purāṇa (Venkateshwara ed.; Pretakalpa cited as 2.chapter.verse)
summary: The classical Purāṇic manual of dying and the afterlife: the signs and pains of death, the thumb-sized person led off by Yama's messengers, the airy conveyance-body and the body built by the ten days' piṇḍas, the year-long road, the Vaitaraṇī, judgment, the preta state and its release through the sons' rites, gifts to the dying, and the means of liberation.

title: Garuḍa Purāṇa Sāroddhāra

attribution.tradition: The 'extracted essence' of the Garuḍa's teaching on the dead, read aloud in households during the days of mourning.
attribution.scholarly: A later compilation of 16 chapters from the Pretakalpa ascribed to Navanidhirāma (Naunidhirāma); translated by E. Wood and S. V. Subrahmanyam (1911).

structure.description: 16 chapters

notes: Compiler's name and date not verified - low confidence; kept as the text actually recited in mourning in North India.
summary: A sixteen-chapter digest of the Garuḍa's teaching on death: the miseries of sinners, the road and city of Yama, the hells, rebirth and embryonic suffering, gifts and rites at death, the ten days, sapiṇḍīkaraṇa, and the conduct that leads to heaven or liberation.

title: Gautama Dharmasūtra
summary: A Dharmasūtra not attached to a surviving Kalpasūtra (associated with the Sāmaveda). It opens 'the Veda is the root of dharma' (1.1), reports that some allow a choice among the life-orders while 'the teachers' hold there is only one, the householder's, because only it is directly enjoined in the Veda (3.1, 3.36), lists the forty sacraments and the eight virtues of the self and declares that the virtues, not the sacraments alone, lead to Brahman (8.14–25), makes regional, caste and family customs authoritative where not contrary to the Veda (11.20), and gives the means of expiation (19.11–12).

scholarly.text: c. 2nd c. BCE (recent estimate; older estimates c. 600–400 BCE)

title: Gāyatrī (Sāvitrī) mantra (Ṛgveda 3.62.10)
summary: The verse to Savitṛ in the gāyatrī metre: 'we meditate on that excellent radiance of the god Savitṛ; may he impel our thoughts (dhī)'. Prefixed with Oṃ and the three vyāhṛtis (bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ) as in VS 36.3, it is the mantra given at initiation (upanayana) and repeated in the twilight worship; the tradition calls it the mother of the Vedas.

attribution.tradition: seen by visvamitra; deity: Savitṛ (Sarvānukramaṇī)
attribution.scholarly: a hymn of the Ṛgveda; books 1 and 10 are among its later layers

title: Gītābhāṣya of Śaṅkara

attribution.tradition: By Ādi Śaṅkarācārya.
attribution.scholarly: Generally accepted as Śaṅkara's.

tradition.text: Śaṅkara, 788–820 CE (most maṭha traditions; some give 509–477 BCE)

summary: The oldest extant complete commentary on the Gītā. Its introduction distinguishes the dharma of activity (pravṛtti) and of withdrawal (nivṛtti) and holds that the Gītā's purport is the highest good attained through steadfastness in knowledge of the self together with renunciation of all works; action performed as offering to the Lord purifies the mind for that knowledge; it rejects the combination of knowledge and works (jñāna-karma-samuccaya) as the means to liberation.

alt_summary: Śaṅkara's commentary on the Gītā: its introduction distinguishes the Vedic dharma of activity (pravṛtti) and of withdrawal (nivṛtti); it argues at length (introducing 2.11 and 3.1) against the combination of knowledge and works, reads selfless action as purifying the mind for knowledge, and treats knowledge culminating in renunciation as the direct means to liberation.

title: Gopatha Brāhmaṇa
summary: The only surviving Brāhmaṇa of the Atharvaveda. It opens with Brahman, the self-existent, alone in the beginning, who creates a second god from himself (1.1.1), tells of the origin of Atharvan and the Aṅgirases and of the Atharvaveda as the Veda of the brahman priest, discusses Oṃ at length, gives rules for the Vedic student, and in its later part explains Śrauta rites, often in words shared with other Brāhmaṇas.

title: Gorakh Bānī
summary: The Hindi (old Hindi / Sadhukkaḍī) sayings ascribed to Gorakhnāth: sabadīs (couplet-sayings), pads (songs) and short works such as the Machhīndra Gorakh Bodh, Ātma Bodh, Narvai Bodh, Abhai Mātrā Jog, Sisṭ Purāṇ, Pandrah Tithi, Sapt Vār and Romāvalī. They teach the yogī's restraint and middle way, the guru, the unstruck sound, the sky-circle and its inverted well of nectar, the retention of bindu, the conquest of death by 'dying the death Gorakh died', and the rejection of temple, mosque and caste.

title: Gorakṣaśataka
summary: 'The hundred of Gorakṣa': a short haṭha manual of six-limbed yoga (posture, breath-control, withdrawal, concentration, meditation, samādhi). It teaches siddhāsana and padmāsana, the centres, ten channels and ten breaths, the awakening of kuṇḍalinī, five seals and locks, the sun and moon and the reversed practice, the five element-concentrations, meditation with and without qualities, and samādhi as the one taste of breath and mind.

attribution.tradition: Spoken by Gorakṣa for the release from the noose of existence (v. 1).
attribution.scholarly: Several different texts carry this title. The text printed by Kuvalayananda and Shukla (and, in a longer form, by Nowotny) is identified by scholars as a recension of the Vivekamārtaṇḍa family; the 'original Gorakṣaśataka' is a different text (src:goraksasataka-mallinson).

structure.description: 101 verses in the Kuvalayananda–Shukla edition (GRETIL numbering, vv. 81 and 95 not numbered in the e-text)

editions.name: Gorakṣaśataka, ed. Swami Kuvalayananda and S. A. Shukla (Lonavla: Kaivalyadhama); GRETIL e-text

notes: Refs in this shard follow the Kuvalayananda–Shukla (GRETIL) numbering. U28 may add the haṭha analysis.

title: Gorakṣaśataka (recension printed by Briggs)
summary: The Gorakṣaśataka in the recension printed by G. W. Briggs (1938) and found as the first hundred verses of the Gorakṣapaddhati: after praising Mīnanātha it teaches the six limbs, the two postures, the knowledge of the six centres, sixteen supports, three aims and five voids of one's own body, the channels and breaths, and ends with the purification of the channels by alternate breathing.

structure.description: 101 verses (Muktabodha e-text M00522); numbering runs about three verses ahead of the Kuvalayananda–Shukla text at the start

title: Gorakṣaśataka (the 'original' Gorakṣaśataka)
summary: A distinct text transmitted under the same title, identified and translated by J. Mallinson as the original Gorakṣaśataka: a manual of about a hundred verses teaching yoga through the control of the breath, the stirring of Sarasvatī (sarasvatīcālana), several kinds of breath retention and the three locks; several of its verses reappear in the Haṭhapradīpikā.

editions.name: J. Mallinson, 'The Original Gorakṣaśataka', in D. G. White (ed.), Yoga in Practice (Princeton, 2012)

notes: Id disambiguated by editor per the data model. Contents recalled in outline only; not available locally.

title: Govinda-bhāṣya
summary: Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa's commentary on the Brahma Sūtras for the Gauḍīya school, reading them as teaching Kṛṣṇa (Govinda) as Brahman, the reality of the world and souls, and devotion as the means; it uses Madhva's category of viśeṣa to explain the unity of the Lord and his attributes.

attribution.tradition: written at Galta (Jaipur) at Govindadeva's command in a dream, to establish the Gauḍīyas' own Brahma Sūtra commentary
attribution.scholarly: composed in the context of the early-18th-c. Jaipur examinations of Gauḍīya orthodoxy

title: Govindalīlāmṛta
summary: Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja's Sanskrit poem on Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa's pastimes through the eight periods of the day (aṣṭakālīya-līlā).

title: Grāmageya-gāna (Veyagāna)
summary: The first song-book of the Kauthuma–Rāṇāyanīya Sāmaveda: the melodies on the Pūrvārcika verses 'to be sung in the village', i.e. in public ritual; it shows how each verse is transformed into a sāman with stretched vowels, repetitions and stobhas.

title: Gūḍhārthadīpikā
summary: Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's commentary on the Bhagavad Gītā, reading its three hexads as the sections on works, devotion/meditation and knowledge, and joining Advaita with an intense devotion to Kṛṣṇa.
alt_summary: Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Advaita commentary on the Gītā, which also exalts devotion; it divides the Gītā into three sections of six chapters — action, devotion (upāsanā) and knowledge — corresponding to the three parts of the Veda and to the words 'thou', 'that' and 'art' of the great saying.

title: Guptavatī

attribution.tradition: Bhāskararāya's commentary on the Saptaśatī.
attribution.scholarly: An 18th-c. Śrīvidyā reading of the Devī Māhātmya.

summary: A Śrīvidyā commentary on the Devī Māhātmya, with its mantra-structure and recitation.

title: Guru Gītā
location_in_parent: claimed for the Skanda Purāṇa, Uttarakhaṇḍa, as a dialogue of Umā and Maheśvara

attribution.tradition: Śiva's teaching to Pārvatī on Mount Kailāsa on the guru, told by Sūta to the sages
attribution.scholarly: a late devotional text in several recensions (c. 180 to over 350 verses); its place in the Skanda Purāṇa is not borne out by the standard printed editions (low)

tradition.text: spoken by Śiva on Kailāsa

structure.description: recensions differ: the Ganeshpuri (Siddha Yoga) recension numbers 182 verses plus preliminary and closing verses; a Kashi 1920 edition prints about 230; three-chapter versions of about 350 verses exist

summary: Śiva teaches that the guru is Brahman itself: the syllable 'gu' is darkness and 'ru' its remover; the guru is Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheśvara and the supreme Brahman; the root of meditation is the guru's form, of worship his feet, of mantra his word, of liberation his grace. Without knowing the guru-principle, sacrifices, vows and pilgrimages are fruitless; the teaching is secret and to be given only to the devoted.

editions.name: Śrī Guru Gītā, Shree Gurudev Ashram, Ganeshpuri (sanskrit/raw_etexts digitization)
Gurugītā with Hindi, Bhārata Dharma Mahāmaṇḍala, Kashi 1920 (eBhāratī Sampat Ebharati-6674)

notes: Chanted daily in the Siddha Yoga tradition of Muktananda (recent) and widely in guru-centred circles.

title: Guruparamparāprabhāvam (Ārāyirappaṭi)
summary: The Maṇipravāḷa hagiography of the Āḻvārs and ācāryas attributed to Piṉpaḻagiya Perumāḷ Jīyar: the source of the stories of Nāthamuni's recovery of the Prabandham, Yāmuna's three folded fingers, Rāmānuja's teachers and the six sayings of Varadarāja.

title: Guruparamparāprabhāvam (Mūvāyirappaṭi)
summary: The Vaṭakalai hagiography of the teacher lineage, the 'Three Thousand', traditionally attributed to the third Brahmatantra Svatantra Jīyar.
notes: Attribution recalled with low confidence: the tradition names 'the third' holder of the Brahmatantra Svatantra title, not necessarily Deśika's own disciple.

title: Haṃsa Gītā

scholarly.text: composed and expanded in stages, c. 4th c. BCE – 4th c. CE

summary: Prajāpati in the form of a golden swan teaches the Sādhyas: truth, self-restraint and forbearance, not returning abuse for abuse, and guarding the door of speech.

title: Haṃsa Gītā (Bhāgavata)

attribution.tradition: the Lord in the form of a swan (Haṃsa) answers the four Kumāras (Sanaka and his brothers) before Brahmā; recorded by Vyāsa in the Bhāgavata
attribution.scholarly: part of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa

tradition.text: composed by Vyāsa and recited by Śuka to Parīkṣit at the opening of the Kali age (traditional reckoning from 3102 BCE)

scholarly.text: c. 9th-10th c. CE (South India); some scholars allow earlier layers

summary: Answers the Kumāras' question how the mind and the guṇas can be separated: the question 'who are you?' has no footing where the self is one; waking, dream and sleep are states of the intellect of which the self is the witness; abiding in the fourth (turya) the knower sees the world as the mind's play, like a whirling firebrand, and the body continues only while its karma lasts.

title: Haṃsa Gītā (Mahābhārata)

attribution.tradition: Prajāpati in the form of a golden swan, teaching the Sādhyas
attribution.scholarly: a named teaching passage ('gītā') of the Mahābhārata

summary: The swan teaches forbearance, truthfulness, self-control and not returning insult for insult as the way to the highest.

title: Haṃsa Upaniṣad

canon.group_scheme: editorial grouping of the 108 used by the Adyar Library series and most modern catalogues; the Muktikā itself lists the 108 by Veda only

attribution.tradition: Śruti: revealed, without human author (apauruṣeya); the Muktikā presents it as one of the 108 Upaniṣads that Rāma teaches Hanumān, each belonging to a Vedic śākhā
attribution.scholarly: anonymous; assigned to a Veda by the Muktikā list, not by any surviving śākhā transmission

tradition.text: Śruti: eternal and authorless; no human date

scholarly.text: Scholarly accounts differ by text. Several Yoga Upaniṣads (e.g. Amṛtabindu, Amṛtanāda, Kṣurikā, Tejobindu, Nādabindu, Dhyānabindu, Brahmavidyā, Yogatattva, Yogaśikhā, Haṃsa) survive in shorter northern versions that are older; the expanded southern recensions (as in this collection) borrow from medieval haṭha works and were probably compiled in South India, perhaps as late as the 18th c. (Bouy 1994).

summary: Gautama asks Sanatsujāta (in this recension) for the knowledge Śiva gave Pārvatī: the haṃsa (the self as the natural breath-mantra haṃsa/so'ham) pervading all bodies, its ascent through the centres, the mantra's seer, metre and deity, the eight-petalled heart lotus whose directions govern moods, and the ten inner sounds with their effects, ending in becoming Brahman.

title: Haṃsadūta

title: Haribhaktivilāsa
summary: The Gauḍīya code of Vaiṣṇava ritual and conduct in twenty 'vilāsas': the guru and disciple and their testing, initiation, daily purity and worship, deity worship with nyāsa and bhūta-śuddhi, the name and offences, the Ekādaśī fast and festivals, temple construction and consecration.

attribution.tradition: compiled by Gopāla Bhaṭṭa (named in the text) with Sanātana's commentary Digdarśinī; some accounts credit Sanātana with the compilation itself
attribution.scholarly: authorship division disputed

title: Harikathāmṛtasāra
summary: Jagannātha Dāsa's Kannada poem setting out Dvaita theology — Hari's supremacy, the gradation of souls and deities, the Lord's presence in all things and the means of liberation — in the Haridāsa tradition.
notes: Owned in substance by U56 (Karnataka Haridāsas); listed here for its Dvaita doctrine.

title: Harināmāmṛtavyākaraṇa
summary: Jīva's Sanskrit grammar in which every technical term is replaced by names of Kṛṣṇa, so that learning grammar is remembering the Lord.

title: Hariścandra Kāvya (Rāghavāṅka)
summary: Rāghavāṅka's ṣaṭpadi retelling of King Hariścandra's trials for the sake of truth; a classic of the Vīraśaiva poets, though not a doctrinal Vīraśaiva work.

title: Hārīta Gītā

title: Hārīta Dharmasūtra / Hārītasmṛti (fragments)

notes: The brahmavādinī/sadyovadhū quotation is known through later digests; wording not verified here.

title: Harivaṃśa
location_in_parent: Supplement (khila) appended to the Mahābhārata; critical edition in 118 chapters with appendices

attribution.tradition: Composed by Vyāsa as the khila of the Bhārata; recited by Vaiśampāyana to Janamejaya.
attribution.scholarly: A later supplement to the epic.

tradition.text: Vyāsa, end of the Dvāpara yuga

structure.description: Critical edition (BORI 1969–71) of about 118 chapters in three parts (Harivaṃśa, Viṣṇu, Bhaviṣya parvans in the vulgate).

summary: The 'lineage of Hari', the supplement (khila) to the Mahābhārata: the genealogy of the Vṛṣṇis, creation accounts, and the life of Kṛṣṇa from birth, including his youth among the cowherds of Vraja, to his deeds at Mathurā and Dvārakā.

notes: Chapter count of the critical text given from memory (low confidence).
alt_summary: Creation and the dynasties, then Kṛṣṇa's birth, childhood in Vraja (including the hallīsaka dance with the cowherd women), deeds at Mathurā and Dvārakā; the Purāṇic life of Kṛṣṇa that the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata Purāṇas expand.

summary: Bāṇa's account of Harṣa and his ancestors. Chapter 3 tells how king Puṣpabhūti, a devout Māheśvara, honoured Bhairavācārya, a great Śaiva from the south with thousands of disciples, and assisted him in a night rite in the great cremation ground.

editions.name: Digital Corpus of Sanskrit (DCS) text

notes: Listed under the Kāpālikas because scholarship discusses Bhairavācārya among portraits of skull-and-cremation-ground Śaiva ascetics; the text itself calls him a great Śaiva (mahāśaiva), not a Kāpālika.

title: Hastāmalakīya (Hastāmalaka-stotra)
summary: Twelve (or fourteen) verses ascribed to Hastāmalaka, answering Śaṅkara's question 'who are you?' by declaring himself the eternal consciousness that, like the sun, illumines mind and senses; a commentary is ascribed to Śaṅkara.

title: Hayagrīvastotra

title: Hīr (Wāris Shāh)

notes: Sufi-context literature, used as context only for the depiction of Nāth practice.

title: Hiraṇyagarbha Sūkta (Ṛgveda 10.121)
summary: The hymn with the refrain 'to which god shall we offer with oblation?' (kasmai devāya haviṣā vidhema): the Golden Germ arose in the beginning, born the one lord of what exists; he holds earth and heaven; he gives self and strength; his shadow is immortality and death; the great waters bearing the germ brought forth Agni, and from them arose the one life-breath of the gods; the last verse names him Prajāpati.

attribution.tradition: seen by hiranyagarbha-prajapatya; deity: Ka (Prajāpati) (Sarvānukramaṇī)
attribution.scholarly: a hymn of the Ṛgveda; books 1 and 10 are among its later layers

notes: The tradition reads the interrogative 'ka' (who?) as a name of Prajāpati. Verse 10 is widely held to be a later addition and is omitted in the Padapāṭha (as usually reported). Also VS 23.1 and TS 4.1.8 (checked).

title: Hiraṇyakeśi Dharmasūtra

title: Hiraṇyakeśi Gṛhyasūtra

summary: One of the three gems of the Pāñcarātra, in 33 paṭalas. Sages ask Śāṇḍilya, who relates Bhagavān's teaching to Nārada. An additional passage in the printed text names the three gems and their expansions (Pādma, Pārameśvara, Īśvara) and assigns them to Kāñcī, Śrīraṅgam and Melkote.

title: Kāmasūtra of Vātsyāyana
summary: The śāstra of the third aim. Its second chapter teaches that a man with a span of a hundred years should divide his time and pursue the three aims so that they support and do not harm one another — learning and wealth in youth, love in early manhood, dharma and liberation in old age (1.2.1–4) — that of the three each earlier is weightier (1.2.14), and answers objections of Mīmāṃsakas and of Lokāyatikas, who say dharma's fruit is future and doubtful: 'better a pigeon today than a peacock tomorrow' (1.2.21–24).

Lists checked by the Phase-B author against local e-texts: Kāmika pūrva 1.30–92 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/Kamikagama.md (Kāmika Pūrvabhāga, Madras 1909 Grantha ed. as transcribed)), Kiraṇa vidyāpāda 10.3–27 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/kiranagama.md (Kiraṇa vidyāpāda, South Indian printed text as transcribed)) and the Śrīkaṇṭhīya list quoted by Jayaratha on TĀ 1.18 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/tantrAlokaH_viveka-vyAkhyA-sahitaH-1.md (Tantrāloka with Jayaratha's Viveka, KSTS vol. 1)).
summary: No. 27 of the 28 Śaiva Siddhānta mūlāgamas (Rudrabheda). According to the Kāmika it was first received by Devavibhava (Kiraṇa: Devapitṛ), then the sage Saṃvartaka. The Kāmika assigns it 9 upabheda(s): Gāruḍa, Nairṛta, Nīla, Rūkṣa, Bhānuka, Dhenuka, Prabuddha, Buddha, Kāla. A dialogue in which Garuḍa questions Śiva. An old Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript is dated 924 CE (scholarly report). Its vidyāpāda (12 paṭalas: paśu, māyā, karma, pati, śaktipāta, dīkṣā, mantra, bhuvana, śivatattva, tantrāvatāra, mātṛkā, yantra) is an early statement of Siddhānta doctrine.

attribution.scholarly: A composite work of many hands grown over several centuries around a narrative core; the frame narratives and the didactic books (esp. Śānti and Anuśāsana) are generally held to be later layers.

tradition.text: composed by Vyāsa at the close of the Dvāpara yuga, before the Kali yuga (traditionally reckoned from 3102 BCE)

structure.description: 18 books (parvans), traditionally 100 sub-books (upaparvans) as listed in the Parvasaṃgraha (1.2); the Harivaṃśa is its supplement (khila). The tradition speaks of 100,000 verses (śatasāhasrī saṃhitā); 1.1.61 says Vyāsa made a 24,000-verse Bhārata without the sub-stories (upākhyānas); 1.1.50 records three starting points used by reciters (Manu, Āstīka, Uparicara). The critical text as digitized locally has 2,097 chapters and about 73,800 verse units.

summary: The great epic of the Bhārata war between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas, calling itself a 'fifth Veda' (kārṣṇa veda) and a treatise on dharma, artha, kāma and mokṣa; besides the narrative it contains extended teaching sections (the Bhagavad Gītā, the Rājadharma, Āpaddharma and Mokṣadharma of the Śāntiparvan, the Anugītā, the Sanatsujātīya, Vidura's counsel, the Yakṣa's questions, the Nārāyaṇīya). It says of itself that what is found here on the four aims of life is found elsewhere, and what is not here is nowhere (1.56.33).

summary: one of the thirty-seven works of Madhva collected as the Sarvamūla ('root of all'); a verse work in thirty-two chapters: the first sets out the purport of all scripture (Viṣṇu's supremacy, the five differences, the gradation of souls, bhakti as the means); the second the principles of interpretation, including the threefold meaning of the Mahābhārata; the third creation; and the rest retell the Rāmāyaṇa and the Mahābhārata, including Kṛṣṇa's life, in the light of that purport. Several Yoga Upaniṣads (e.g. Amṛtabindu, Amṛtanāda, Kṣurikā, Tejobindu, Nādabindu, Dhyānabindu, Brahmavidyā, Yogatattva, Yogaśikhā, Haṃsa) survive in shorter northern versions that are older; the expanded southern recensions (as in this collection) borrow from medieval haṭha works and were probably compiled in South India, perhaps as late as the 18th c. summary: Sureśvara's treatise (verse with prose) establishing 'actionlessness': ch. 1 refutes the view that works, alone or combined with knowledge, lead to liberation; ch. 2 separates the self from the not-self by agreement and difference; ch. 3 explains how 'tat tvam asi' gives immediate knowledge; ch. 4 summarizes and describes the knower, whose virtues arise without effort and who cannot act licentiously.

title: Nandikeśvara-kāśikā

summary: Vātsyāyana's commentary, the oldest extant on the Nyāya Sūtra. summary: The root text of Nyāya. It opens by promising the highest good (niḥśreyasa) from knowledge of the truth of sixteen categories (NS 1.1.1), states the chain from false knowledge to liberation (1.1.2), defines the four means of knowledge, the twelve objects of knowledge beginning with the self, the five-membered demonstration, debate, pseudo-reasons, quibbles, futile rejoinders and points of defeat (book 1); examines the means of knowledge (book 2), the self, body, senses, cognition and mind (book 3), faults, rebirth, fruit, pain, liberation, the whole and atoms, rival views such as momentariness and idealism, and the yogic means to knowledge of truth (book 4); and lists the twenty-four futile rejoinders and twenty-two points of defeat (book 5).

summary: Vyāsatīrtha's great polemic against Advaita, in four chapters that follow the four chapters of the Brahmasūtras: (1) the reality of the world — a refutation of the five Advaita definitions of falsity (mithyātva) and of the inferences from perceivability, insentience and limitedness; (2) the Upaniṣads do not teach an impartite, attributeless meaning, and the flawless Brahman is absolutely different from the flawed souls; (3) the means — against the Vivaraṇa view of hearing, reflection and meditation, the Lord is to be won by direct realization born of meditation; (4) liberation is not the mere cessation of ignorance, and the liberated, from Brahmā and Rudra down, are graded. Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Advaitasiddhi answers it point by point.

title: Nyāyaratnamālā

title: Nyāyasāra

structure.description: 3 paricchedas (pratyakṣa, anumāna, āgama)

summary: Bhāsarvajña's manual in three chapters (perception, inference, verbal testimony): it accepts only three means of knowledge, treats yogic perception, and holds — against the mainstream — that liberation is the absolute cessation of pain together with the experience of eternal bliss; its last part links the path to Śaiva yoga.

title: Nyāyasiddhāñjana
summary: Deśika's treatise on the categories of Viśiṣṭādvaita — insentient substance, soul, Lord, the eternal realm, cognition and non-substances.

tradition.text: Vedānta Deśika, 1268–1369 CE (traditional)

title: Nyāyasiddhāntadīpa
summary: Śaśadhara's pre-Gaṅgeśa treatise on Nyāya topics.

title: Nyāyasiddhāntamuktāvalī

scholarly.text: first half of the 17th c. CE

summary: Viśvanātha's auto-commentary on the Bhāṣāpariccheda, the standard intermediate text of syncretic Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika in Navya-Nyāya idiom (e.g. its inference of a maker from the effecthood of earth, sprouts and the like).

title: Nyāyasūcīnibandha

scholarly.text: 841 CE (if Vikrama era) or 976 CE (if Śaka era)

summary: Vācaspati Miśra's index of the sūtras and prakaraṇas of the Nyāya Sūtra, which fixed the sūtra text as read by the later tradition; its closing verse gives a date (year 898 of an unnamed era).

title: Nyāyasudhā
summary: Jayatīrtha's great commentary on Madhva's Anuvyākhyāna, the most authoritative exposition of Dvaita doctrine and polemic, esteemed in the tradition as its central scholastic text; it expands Madhva's arguments against Advaita, Buddhist, Jain, Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, Mīmāṃsā and Sāṃkhya positions.

title: Nyāyasudhā-parimala

tradition.text: Rāghavendra entered his brindāvana at Mantrālaya in 1671

summary: Rāghavendra Tīrtha's commentary on Jayatīrtha's Nyāyasudhā, from which he is called Parimalācārya.

title: Nyāyasudhā (Rāṇaka)
notes: Distinct from Jayatīrtha's Dvaita Nyāyasudhā (src:nyayasudha).
summary: Someśvara Bhaṭṭa's commentary on Kumārila's Tantravārttika, known as Rāṇaka.

title: Nyāyasūtravṛtti (Viśvanātha)

scholarly.text: 1634 CE (date given in the text, as usually reported)

summary: Viśvanātha Nyāyapañcānana's running commentary on the Nyāya Sūtra, in Navya-Nyāya idiom.

title: Nyāyatattva
summary: Nāthamuni's lost work on logic and the means of knowledge, which later Viśiṣṭādvaita logicians (Vedānta Deśika's Nyāyapariśuddhi) say they follow; known only from citations.

tradition.text: Nāthamuni, traditionally 9th–10th c. (hagiographies give an extremely long life)

title: Nyāyavivaraṇa

attribution.tradition: Madhva (Ānandatīrtha), counted among his thirty-seven works
attribution.scholarly: accepted as Madhva's

tradition.text: composed by Madhva (Ānandatīrtha); the tradition dates his life to 1199–1278 or 1238–1317

summary: one of the thirty-seven works of Madhva collected as the Sarvamūla ('root of all'); a short prose work setting out, adhikaraṇa by adhikaraṇa, the reasoning (nyāya) by which Madhva reads the Brahmasūtras.

title: Oṉpatiṉāyirappaṭi (the 'Nine Thousand')
summary: Nañjīyar's Maṇipravāḷa commentary on the Tiruvāymoḻi; the tradition says the copy made by Nampiḷḷai was lost in the Kāvēri and rewritten by him from memory.

title: Oṣadhi Sūkta (Ṛgveda 10.97)
summary: The physician's hymn to the healing plants, born three ages before the gods; where plants gather like kings in assembly, that inspired one is called a physician, slayer of demons and dispeller of disease.

attribution.scholarly: a hymn of the Ṛgveda; books 1 and 10 are among its later layers

title: Oupnek'hat
summary: Anquetil-Duperron's Latin rendering (1801–1802) of the Persian Sirr-i Akbar; the first Upaniṣad collection widely read in Europe.

title: Padacandrikā of Anantadeva
summary: A short word-by-word commentary on the sūtras by Anantadeva, who says he made this Padacandrikā after examining 'the vṛtti on the meaning of the sūtras' and offers it at the feet of Śiva (closing verse); it glosses nirodha as the mind's inward dissolution into its cause (1.2).
notes: Date not established (gap).

title: Padamañjarī
summary: Haradatta's sub-commentary on the Kāśikāvṛtti.
notes: Whether this Haradatta is the Dharmasūtra commentator of the same name is uncertain.

title: Padaratnāvalī
summary: Vijayadhvaja Tīrtha's word-by-word commentary on the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, the standard Mādhva commentary on it.

title: Padārthādarśa
summary: Rāghavabhaṭṭa's commentary on the Śāradātilaka, rich in quotations from lost tantras.

title: Padārthadharmasaṅgraha
summary: Praśastapāda's systematic exposition of Vaiśeṣika (often called Praśastapādabhāṣya, though not a line-by-line commentary): after saluting Īśvara and Kaṇāda it declares knowledge of the similarities and dissimilarities of the six categories the cause of the highest good, arising from dharma manifested by the Lord's command; it fixes twenty-four qualities, gives the account of cosmic dissolution and creation by Maheśvara's will, divides cognition into knowledge (perception, inference, memory, seers' knowledge) and its opposites, treats yogic perception, dharma and adharma, and liberation.
notes: Commentaries: Vyomaśiva's Vyomavatī, Śrīdhara's Nyāyakandalī, Udayana's Kiraṇāvalī, and later ones.

title: Padārthatattvanirūpaṇa
summary: Raghunātha Śiromaṇi's critical re-examination of the Vaiśeṣika list of categories, proposing reductions and additions to the traditional seven.
notes: The specific revisions (e.g. treatment of space, time and ultimate particularity) are recalled with low confidence and are not asserted as teachings in this skeleton.

title: Padma Purāṇa

attribution.tradition: Compiled by Vyāsa (Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana) from the one primeval Purāṇa and taught through Romaharṣaṇa and his line. Told of the time when the world was a golden lotus (Matsya 53.14).
attribution.scholarly: Survives in two main recensions - a Bengal recension in five khaṇḍas and a South Indian/Ānandāśrama recension in six khaṇḍas (the Venkateshwara print arranges Sṛṣṭi, Bhūmi, Svarga, Brahma, Pātāla, Uttara and Kriyāyogasāra); many layers of different date.

tradition.text: Vyāsa, end of Dvāpara

structure.description: khaṇḍas differing by recension; 55,000 verses by the traditional count (BhP 12.13.4; Matsya 53.14)

notes: Contains the Bhāgavata-māhātmya (Uttarakhaṇḍa; colophon checked in the local e-text), the Gītā-māhātmya, the Śiva Gītā (U06), the classification of the Purāṇas by the three guṇas (Uttarakhaṇḍa; ch. number edition-dependent, often cited as 236.18-21), and the list of ten offences against the name as cited by Gauḍīya authors.
summary: A vast Vaiṣṇava-leaning compendium: creation, tīrthas (Puṣkara and others), vratas (Ekādaśī, Kārttika, Māgha), the glory of the Bhāgavata and the Gītā, Rāma narratives, the worship of the name and of the śālagrāma and tulasī, and the guṇa-classification of the eighteen Purāṇas.

title: Pādma Saṃhitā

attribution.tradition: revealed by Bhagavān (Nārāyaṇa/Vāsudeva); one of the traditional 108 saṃhitās

summary: Pāñcarātra saṃhitā in the four pādas (jñāna, yoga, kriyā, caryā), presented as the expansion of the Jayākhya and followed in practice at Hastiśaila (Kāñcī). Its jñānapāda praises the Pāñcarātra above all śāstras, explains the name (other systems become 'night' before it) and divides it into four siddhāntas (1.60–83).

title: Padmāvat
summary: Malik Muhammad Jāyasī's Avadhi epic (1540), in which King Ratansen takes the yogī's guise — earrings, patched cloak, horn and begging bowl — to seek Padmāvatī; context for the Nāth insignia in the 16th century.
notes: Sufi-context literature, context only.

title: Pādukāsahasra
summary: Deśika's 1,008 verses in 32 sections (paddhati) on the sandals of Raṅganātha, composed, the tradition says, in a single night; the sandals are Nammāḻvār (Śaṭhakopa) and the teacher who carries the Lord to the devotee.

title: Pañcadaśī

attribution.tradition: Vidyāraṇya; some accounts ascribe part of the work to Bhāratītīrtha
attribution.scholarly: Vidyāraṇya (with possible co-authorship)

structure.description: 15 chapters in three groups of five

summary: Vidyāraṇya's fifteen-chapter verse manual in three pentads — five 'discriminations' (viveka: of reality, the elements, the sheaths, duality, the great sayings), five 'lamps' (dīpa: the picture, contentment, the immutable, meditation, the theatre) and five 'blisses' (ānanda: of yoga, of the self, of non-duality, of knowledge, of objects). It distinguishes māyā (pure sattva) as the adjunct of Īśvara from avidyā (impure sattva) as the adjunct of the jīva, and gives the canvas, four-space, tenth-man and theatre-lamp illustrations and the seven states of the jīva.

title: Pañcapādikā

attribution.tradition: Padmapāda; the name 'five pādas' and the tradition that the rest was destroyed (his uncle burnt the manuscript, Śaṅkaradigvijaya) explain why only the opening survives

summary: Padmapāda's commentary on the adhyāsa-bhāṣya and the first four sūtras of Śaṅkara's BSBh: analyses the definition of superimposition, presents ignorance as an insentient power (avidyā-śakti) that is the material cause of superimposition, glosses 'mithyā' as 'indescribable', and treats the jīva as a reflection of Brahman in the ego.

title: Pañcapādikāvivaraṇa
summary: Prakāśātman's sub-commentary on the Pañcapādikā, founding text of the Vivaraṇa school: Brahman is the locus and object of a positive (bhāva-rūpa) indescribable ignorance, established by perception, inference and presumption; the jīva is the reflection of Brahman, real and identical with its prototype; hearing is the principal means, enjoined by a restrictive injunction; the mahāvākya yields immediate knowledge.

title: Pañcapadyāni

title: Pañcārthabhāṣya

attribution.tradition: 'Composed by the revered Kauṇḍinya' (colophon of each adhyāya).
attribution.scholarly: Kauṇḍinya, c. 4th–6th c. CE. Some scholars have identified him with the Pāśupata tīrthakara Rāśīkara, whose 'bhāṣya' the Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha cites; the identification is uncertain.

structure.description: prose commentary on every sūtra, in five adhyāyas; opens with a verse naming Kauṇḍinya

summary: Kauṇḍinya's commentary reads the Pāśupata Sūtra as teaching five categories (effect, cause, union, rule, end of suffering), defines the Lord, the soul and the bonds, the three means of knowledge, the yamas and niyamas, the six 'doors' of feigned behaviour and the exchange of merit and sin, and correlates the sūtras with a five-stage path (residence, livelihood, strength, action, purification and gain for each stage). It holds that the end of suffering comes by the Lord's grace and that the Lord does not depend on karma.

summary: The standard treatise of Vedic phonetics (śikṣā): it counts sixty-three or sixty-four phonemes declared by Svayambhū (v. 3), explains how speech arises when the self, having grasped meanings with the intellect, joins the mind to the wish to speak, the mind strikes the body's fire and the fire impels the breath (vv. 6–9), classifies sounds by place, effort, tone and duration, lists the faults and the virtues of reciters (vv. 32–33), pictures the six Vedāṅgas as the limbs of the Veda (vv. 41–42), warns that a mantra defective in accent or sound harms the sacrificer (v. 52), and ends in homage to Pāṇini, who received the collection of phonemes from Maheśvara (v. 57).

summary: The root text of the Pāśupatas. Adhyāya 1 prescribes the first-stage observance in the temple (ash-bathing thrice daily, lying in ash, wearing the used garland, the six-limbed offering of laughter, song, dance, the ḍuṇḍuṅkāra sound, prostration and muttering) and lists the powers that arise; adhyāyas 2-4 teach worship of Rudra alone, courting dishonour by feigned madness and the transfer of merit and sin, and non-return; adhyāya 5 teaches the solitary yogin in empty houses, caves and cremation grounds, meditation on Oṃ in the heart, constant remembrance of Rudra and the end of suffering by the Lord's grace.

title: Puruṣa Sūkta (Ṛgveda 10.90)
summary: The hymn of the cosmic Person: thousand-headed, thousand-eyed, thousand-footed, covering the earth and exceeding it by ten fingers; all this is Puruṣa, past and future; one quarter of him is all beings, three quarters the immortal in heaven; from him Virāj was born and from Virāj he; the gods sacrificed Puruṣa as the oblation, and from that sacrifice came the verses, chants, metres and formulas, the animals, the four varṇas from his mouth, arms, thighs and feet, the moon from his mind, the sun from his eye, Indra and Agni from his mouth, wind from his breath, and the worlds; 'with the sacrifice the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice; these were the first dharmas'.

attribution.tradition: seen by narayana-rsi; deity: Puruṣa (Sarvānukramaṇī)
attribution.scholarly: a hymn of the Ṛgveda; books 1 and 10 are among its later layers

notes: Also Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 31.1–16 (with the six 'Uttaranārāyaṇa' verses 31.17–22), Atharvaveda (Śaunaka) 19.6 and Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.12 (last two from memory). Its sixteen verses are used for the sixteen-fold worship in later temple and domestic ritual.

summary: After one's duties have purified the mind, one should approach a true guru: ignorance is the root of rebirth and only knowledge removes it, not action, so knowledge cannot be combined with ritual action; the meaning of 'that thou art' is grasped by partial implication; the self is distinct from the three bodies and three states; superimposition is explained; one meditates on the Self, dissolves the syllables of Oṃ into it, lives out prārabdha free of ego and merges in Rāma. Until all is seen as Rāma, one should worship him.

attribution.tradition: Composed by the sage Vālmīki after Nārada told him Rāma's story; the first śloka arose from his grief at a hunter's killing of one of a pair of krauñca birds (1.2.15–18); sung by Rāma's sons Kuśa and Lava.
attribution.scholarly: An oral-bardic work fixed in writing over centuries; the first and seventh books are widely held to be later additions; transmitted in northern and southern recensions.

tradition.text: composed by Vālmīki in the Tretā yuga, in Rāma's own time

scholarly.text: c. 5th c. BCE – 3rd c. CE, in stages; books 2–6 generally held older than books 1 and 7

structure.description: 7 books (kāṇḍas). The poem itself speaks of 24,000 ślokas in 500 sargas, six books and the Uttara (1.4.2, vulgate). The local southern vulgate text has Bāla 77, Ayodhyā 119, Araṇya 75, Kiṣkindhā 67, Sundara 68, Yuddha 128, Uttara 111 sargas. The Baroda critical edition (1960–75) constitutes a shorter text.

summary: The first poem (ādikāvya): the life of Rāma, prince of Ayodhyā — his exile in obedience to his father's word, the abduction of Sītā by Rāvaṇa, the alliance with the monkeys and Hanumān, the war in Laṅkā, his righteous reign, and (in the last book) the banishment of Sītā. It presents Rāma as dharma embodied: truth to one's word, obedience to parents, fraternal loyalty, protection of those who seek refuge, and the king's duty to his subjects.

A second division into 8 aṣṭakas × 8 adhyāyas (64 adhyāyas) and vargas is used for recitation.

title: Sāyaṇa's commentary on the Ṛgveda (Vedārthaprakāśa)
summary: The complete classical commentary on the Ṛgveda, produced at Vijayanagara under Sāyaṇa's direction: it glosses every word, explains each hymn chiefly by its use in the sacrifice (yajña), draws on Yāska, the Brāhmaṇas and earlier commentators, and in its introduction defines the Veda and defends its authority. Most traditional and modern readings of the Ṛgveda start from it.

summary: The word-by-word recitation of the Ṛgveda, ascribed to Śākalya, which undoes the euphonic combinations (sandhi) and marks compound members, so that every word and accent of the continuous text is fixed; it is the basis of the krama and other interwoven recitations and the oldest witness to how the tradition understood each word.

title: Sāṃkhya Kārikā

attribution.tradition: Composed by Īśvarakṛṣṇa, who summarized in āryā verses the doctrine handed down from the supreme sage (Kapila) through Āsuri and Pañcaśikha by a succession of pupils (SK 70–71); its topics are those of the whole Ṣaṣṭitantra (SK 72).
attribution.scholarly: Authorship accepted. Verses 70–72 are not commented on by Gauḍapāda; Paramārtha's Chinese version lacks v. 63 and its commentary remarks that v. 72 is not original; a 73rd verse is found only in the Māṭhara Vṛtti and in one anonymous vṛtti (V1).

scholarly.text: c. 350–450 CE (before Paramārtha's Chinese translation, c. 557–569 CE)

structure.description: 72 āryā verses in the vulgate (69 doctrinal verses and 3 on the transmission); some versions add a 73rd; 'saptati' (seventy) is a round name

summary: The classical root text of Sāṃkhya. Starting from the threefold suffering and the inadequacy of seen and Vedic remedies, it sets out the three means of knowledge, the pre-existence of the effect, the manifest and the unmanifest, the three guṇas, the proofs of prakṛti and of many puruṣas, the emergence of the twenty-five principles, the thirteen instruments and the subtle body, the fifty-fold creation of cognitions, and liberation (kaivalya) through the knowledge 'I am not, not mine, not I'.

summary: A concise commentary on SK 1–69. It presents Kapila as one of Brahmā's seven mind-born sons, born with virtue, knowledge, dispassion and power, who taught the twenty-five principles to Āsuri; names the three kinds of suffering; explains dharma through compassion, giving and the Pātañjala yamas and niyamas; lists the eight powers; details the fifty categories of the creation of cognitions; and argues that neither Īśvara, nature (svabhāva) nor time, but prakṛti, is the world's cause.

summary: The sūtra text of later Sāṃkhya. It restates the Kārikā's system, supplies the illustrative tales the Kārikā omitted, and argues at length against rivals: that Īśvara is not established as creator, that bondage is not due to avidyā, that things are not momentary, that consciousness is not a product of the elements, that the Veda is neither eternal nor authored yet self-valid; it accepts liberation while living and explains meditation as the removal of passion.

alt_summary: A 14th-century Advaita doxography of sixteen systems; its fifth chapter, 'Pūrṇaprajña-darśana', is an early outside summary of Madhva's system (the five differences, Viṣṇu's supremacy, the gradation of souls).

A doxography of sixteen systems, from the Cārvāka through the Buddhist, Jain, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, grammatical, Sāṃkhya and Yoga schools, each refuted by the next, ending with (a reference to) Advaita as the culmination.
notes: Chapter order (Pūrṇaprajña 5th) recalled at moderate confidence.

title: Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (Mādhyandina)
summary: The 'Brāhmaṇa of a hundred paths', the great Brāhmaṇa of the White Yajurveda. It explains the whole Śrauta ritual — new- and full-moon, fire establishment, Agnihotra, ancestral offering, seasonal rites, Soma, royal consecration, the fire-altar (Agnicayana, books 6–10, with its 'secret' in book 10), horse, human and all-sacrifice, the funeral mound, the Pravargya — and teaches the sacrifice as the cosmic Person and year: Prajāpati fell apart after emitting creatures and is rebuilt in the altar. It records the teaching of Śāṇḍilya (10.6.3), the debates of Yājñavalkya at Janaka's court, the debts, the five great sacrifices, upanayana, Vedic self-study, the flood, and ends with the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (14.4–9).

title: Śatarudrīya (Śrī Rudram, Rudrādhyāya)
summary: The litany of homage to Rudra in his hundreds of forms: after asking Rudra to turn his wrath, bow and arrows away and to show his auspicious, non-terrible body (śivā tanūḥ aghorā), it pays homage (namaḥ) to Rudra as lord of paths, forests, hosts and animals, as present in thieves and craftsmen, in the small and the great, in waters, clouds and grass, and ends by placing the countless Rudras on earth far away. Its eighth section contains 'namaḥ śivāya ca śivatarāya ca', the source the Śaiva traditions give for the five-syllable formula.
notes: Used in the agnicayana to pacify Rudra; recited in the tradition as Rudra-japa (Ekādaśa-, Laghu-, Mahā-, Atirudra) and in Śaiva worship. The Jābāla Upaniṣad names śatarudrīya recitation as a means to immortality (reference only).

title: Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi

It sets out Vīraśaiva doctrine as Śivādvaita consistent with Veda and Āgama and maps the path as 101 sthalas (44 on the side of the soul, 57 on the side of the liṅga) under the six great sthalas from bhakta to aikya.

structure.description: 21 chapters (pariccheda); ch. 1 frame and author's lineage; 2–4 descent of Reṇuka and meeting with Agastya; 5–14 the 44 aṅga-sthalas under bhakta (15), māheśvara (9), prasādi (7), prāṇaliṅgi (5), śaraṇa (4), aikya (4); 15–20 the 57 liṅga-sthalas; 21 Reṇuka's dialogue with Vibhīṣaṇa and his return into the liṅga

title: Tantrāloka
summary: Abhinavagupta's encyclopaedic exposition of the Trika on the basis of the Mālinīvijayottara, integrating Kaula and Krama. After defining bondage as ignorance and knowledge as the sole cause of liberation (1.22-23), it orders all Śaiva practice by the four means (chs. 2-5), sets out time, space, the tattvas and the paths of manifestation (6-12), the descent of grace (13), the whole ritual of initiation, consecration, funerary and daily rites (14-28), the secret Kula ritual (29), mantra, maṇḍala and mudrā (30-32), and ends with unification, the harmony of the scriptures, the lineage and the author's account of himself (33-37).

structure.description: 37 āhnikas (chapters), c. 5,800 verses; chapter topics per Abhinavagupta's own table of contents (TĀ 1.278-329) and colophons: 1 vijñānabheda (the kinds of knowledge; knowledge as the cause of liberation; table of contents); 2 anupāya (the means-less); 3 śāmbhavopāya (the reflection of the universe in consciousness; the letters); 4 śāktopāya (purification of thought, sattarka, the wheel of consciousness, the twelve Kālīs, critique of rules); 5 āṇavopāya (meditation, uccāra of prāṇa, the seven ānandas, the five signs, karaṇa, varṇa); 6 kālopāya / kālatattva (time in the breath and its cycles); 7 cakrodaya (the arising of the wheels; mantra and breath counts); 8 deśādhvan (the path of space: the worlds); 9 tattvādhvan (the path of the tattvas); 10 tattvabheda (divisions of the tattvas; the states and the seven pramātṛs); 11 kalādhvan (the path of the kalās; letters and mantras); 12 adhvopayoga (use of the paths); 13 śaktipāta (the descent of power; its grades); 14 dīkṣopakrama (preliminaries of initiation; removal of concealment); 15 samayadīkṣā (initiation into the samaya; the samaya rules); 16 prameya (the putraka initiation and the knowables purified); 17 vikṣipta/extended initiation (cord, purification of the tattvas, burning the bonds); 18 saṅkṣiptadīkṣā (abbreviated initiation); 19 sadyaḥsamutkrānti (initiation bringing immediate departure from the body); 20 tulādīkṣā (initiation by the balance); 21 parokṣadīkṣā (initiation of the absent and the dead); 22 liṅgoddhāra (removal of a prior sectarian mark); 23 abhiṣeka (consecration as teacher or adept); 24 antyeṣṭi (final rites); 25 śrāddha (rites for the dead); 26 sthaṇḍilapūjā (daily worship on a ritual ground; the remaining life of the initiate); 27 liṅgārcā (worship of the liṅga); 28 parva-pavitraka etc. (occasional rites; the gathering of yoginīs; rites for the guru); 29 rahasyavidhi (the secret Kula ritual); 30 mantra (the mantras); 31 maṇḍala; 32 mudrā; 33 ekīkāra (unification of the paths); 34 svarūpapraveśa (entry into one's own nature); 35 śāstrasammelana (the harmony of the scriptures); 36 āyātikrama (the descent of the scripture through the lineage); 37 upādeyabhāva (why this scripture is to be accepted; the author's account of himself)

title: Tirukkuṟaḷ
summary: Tiruvaḷḷuvar's 1,330 couplets (kuṟaḷ-veṇpā) in 133 chapters of ten, in three books: Aṟam (virtue, 38 chapters — preface, the householder's life, the renunciant's life, fate), Poruḷ (wealth and polity, 70 chapters) and Iṉpam/Kāmam (love, 25 chapters). It names no sectarian deity; its ethics of non-killing, abstention from meat, truthfulness, love, gratitude and renunciation are claimed by Śaivas, Jains, Vaiṣṇavas, Buddhists, and as non-sectarian ('the common scripture').

It declares 'love is Śiva' and 'one family, one God', and joins Vedānta and Siddhānta.

summary: Kṛṣṇa instructs Uddhava to renounce attachment, see the world as the Lord's māyā and wander with equal vision. Through the story of Yadu and a young avadhūta brāhmaṇa it teaches learning from twenty-four teachers in nature, then expounds bondage and liberation, holy company, the guṇas, meditation on the Lord, the eighteen siddhis as obstacles, the three yogas of knowledge, action and devotion by disposition, the tattvas, worship (kriyā-yoga), and devotion as the easiest and highest path.

title: Vacana literature (vacana sāhitya)
summary: The corpus of vacanas — short rhythmic Kannada prose-poems, usually closing with the author's signature name (aṅkita) for the Lord — composed by the twelfth-century śaraṇas of Kalyāṇa and by later vacanakāras. They teach devotion to Śiva as the liṅga, the six stages (ṣaṭsthala), the triad of guru, liṅga and jaṅgama, work as worship (kāyaka) and giving (dāsōha), and criticize caste, pollution rules, temple and Vedic ritualism and outward show in favour of lived experience (anubhava).

attribution.tradition: the utterances of the śaraṇas (Basava, Allama Prabhu, Akka Mahādēvi, Cennabasava and some two hundred others, women among them), preserved in palm-leaf bundles and carried to Uḷavi after the Kalyāṇa upheaval

summary: The root text of Vaiśeṣika in ten books. It announces the explanation of dharma — that from which prosperity and the highest good result — and grounds the Veda's authority; lists the nine substances, the qualities and the five motions and defines substance, quality and motion; treats being, universals and particulars, the elements, time, space, the self (with its marks and plurality) and the atomic mind; atoms and perception; motions caused by the unseen (adṛṣṭa); yoga and liberation; ethics of giving, food and ritual observances; inherence; absence; perception, inference and memory; and the seers' knowledge.

title: Vasiṣṭha Dharmasūtra
summary: A Dharmasūtra associated with the Ṛgveda. It places dharma in śruti and smṛti and, failing these, in the practice of the cultured, 'one free of desire' (1.4–6); teaches that the Vedas do not purify one without right conduct, and leave him at death as fledglings leave the nest (6.3); lets a student who has kept his vow enter whichever order he wishes (7.1–3); tells the renouncer to give up all rites but never the Veda (10.4); and ends: 'practise dharma, not adharma; speak truth, not untruth; look far, not near; look to the highest, not to what is not highest' (30.1).
