attribution.tradition: Proclaimed by Vāyu, the wind god, in the Śveta-kalpa, joined with the glory of Rudra (Matsya 53.18); several lists count it fourth in place of the Śiva Purāṇa (Matsya 53.18; Nārada 1.95).
attribution.scholarly: Regarded by most scholars as among the oldest Purāṇas; it shares a common core with the Brahmāṇḍa (the Kūrma list calls the eighteenth 'Vāyavīya ... named Brahmāṇḍa').

tradition.text: Vyāsa, end of Dvāpara

structure.description: four pādas (prakriyā, anuṣaṅga, upodghāta, upasaṃhāra); 24,000 verses by the traditional count (Matsya 53.18)

notes: Contains Pāśupata-yoga chapters, the Gayā-māhātmya (appendix) and śrāddha-kalpa; exact chapter numbers not checked (no local e-text) - low confidence on locators.
summary: An early Śaiva-leaning Purāṇa of the classic type: creation, cosmography, time, manvantaras and genealogies, Pāśupata yoga with its obstacles and powers, śrāddha, and (in an appended portion) the glory of Gayā for the ancestors.

title: Vāyustuti (Harivāyustuti)
summary: A hymn by Trivikrama Paṇḍitācārya praising Vāyu (Mukhyaprāṇa) in his three avatāras — Hanumān, Bhīma and Madhva — as the foremost servant of Hari; recited daily in the tradition, framed by Madhva's two Narasiṃha verses.
notes: Author named in the colophon of the raw_etexts copy.

title: Vedadīpa (Mahīdhara on the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā)
summary: Mahīdhara's commentary on the Mādhyandina Saṃhitā, composed at Vārāṇasī, the standard later commentary of the White Yajurveda, largely following Uvaṭa.

title: Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa
summary: Lagadha's manual of Vedic time-reckoning for fixing the times of sacrifices: a five-year cycle (yuga) of lunar and solar time presided over by Prajāpati, the twenty-seven lunar mansions (nakṣatra), the lunar days, the solstices (the northward turning of sun and moon at the beginning of Śraviṣṭhā), and rules for intercalation. It declares that the Vedas exist for the sacrifices, the sacrifices depend on time, and so this science of time stands at the head of the Vedāṅgas.

attribution.tradition: the teaching of Lagadha, the great-souled (v. 2)
attribution.scholarly: Lagadha, known only from this text

scholarly.text: composition usually placed in the second half of the 1st millennium BCE; the solstitial position it states has been dated by some to the 2nd millennium BCE (disputed)

structure.description: Ārca (Ṛgveda) recension of 36 verses and Yājuṣa recension of 43–44 verses

notes: Commentary on the Yājuṣa recension: Somākara. Later jyotiṣa → U32.

title: Vedāntakalpataru
summary: Amalānanda's sub-commentary on the Bhāmatī, defending and extending its positions.

title: Vedāntakaustubha
summary: Śrīnivāsa's commentary on Nimbārka's Vedāntapārijātasaurabha, the classical exposition of the school's reading of the Brahma Sūtras.

title: Vedāntapārijātasaurabha
summary: Nimbārka's brief commentary on the Brahma Sūtras establishing natural difference-and-non-difference: souls and world are Brahman's powers, different and non-different from him like sun and rays or snake and coils.
notes: Translated by Roma Bose (1940–43) with Śrīnivāsa's Vedāntakaustubha.

title: Vedāntaratnamañjūṣā
summary: Puruṣottamācārya's commentary on the Daśaślokī, systematising the arthapañcaka and the means of attainment.

title: Vedāntasiddhāntamuktāvalī
summary: Prakāśānanda's treatise arguing that the world exists only in being perceived (dṛṣṭi-sṛṣṭi-vāda), that there is one jīva (eka-jīva-vāda), and that ignorance alone accounts for the appearance, with no need of a theory of creation.

title: Vedāntatattvaviveka
summary: Nṛsiṃhāśrama's treatise on the principal topics of Advaita in the Vivaraṇa manner.

title: Vedāntadīpa
summary: Rāmānuja's middle-length commentary on the Brahma Sūtras, clarifying the Śrībhāṣya's reading of each sūtra.

tradition.text: Rāmānuja, 1017–1137 CE (traditional)

title: Vedāntakalpalatikā
summary: Madhusūdana's early treatise on liberation and its means, surveying and refuting other schools' conceptions of liberation.

title: Vedāntaparibhāṣā

structure.description: 8 paricchedas

summary: Dharmarāja Adhvarīndra's manual of Advaita epistemology in eight chapters: perception, inference, comparison, verbal testimony, presumption and non-cognition (the six means of knowledge, following Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā for empirical matters), then the object (Brahman's defining marks, creation and dissolution) and the purpose (liberation and its means).

title: Vedāntasāra
notes: Commentaries: Nṛsiṃha Sarasvatī's Subodhinī (1588), Rāmatīrtha's Vidvanmanorañjanī.
summary: Sadānanda's standard primer: the four preliminaries (qualified student, subject, relation, purpose); superimposition and retraction; ignorance with its two powers, collective and individual, and the three bodies, states and sheaths; quintuplication; a graded refutation of mistaken views of the self; the analysis of 'tat tvam asi' by exclusive-inclusive implication; hearing, reflection, contemplation and samādhi with eight auxiliaries and four obstacles; the jīvanmukta.

title: Vedāntasāra (of Rāmānuja)
summary: A brief commentary by Rāmānuja on the Brahma Sūtras (distinct from Sadānanda's Advaita Vedāntasāra, src:vedantasara).

tradition.text: Rāmānuja, 1017–1137 CE (traditional)

title: Vedāntasāra-Vīraśaiva-Cintāmaṇi

title: Vedārthasaṅgraha
summary: Rāmānuja's independent treatise on the meaning of the Upaniṣads: it criticizes the views of Śaṅkara, Bhāskara and Yādavaprakāśa, classifies scriptural texts into those of difference, non-difference and mediation (ghaṭaka), reads 'tat tvam asi' by co-reference, and establishes Nārāyaṇa as the supreme Brahman reached through bhakti.

attribution.tradition: Rāma's answer to Vibhīṣaṇa, anxious that Rāma fights on foot against Rāvaṇa's chariot

title: Vibhramaviveka
summary: Maṇḍana Miśra's short treatise examining the rival accounts of perceptual error (the khyāti theories) and defending the view that error apprehends a thing as other than it is.
alt_summary: Maṇḍana Miśra's short verse treatise examining the theories of perceptual error (khyāti) of the rival schools.

attribution.scholarly: a named teaching passage ('gītā') of the Mahābhārata

summary: Vicakhnu praises non-violence toward all beings and condemns animal slaughter in sacrifice.
alt_summary: King Vicakhnu, seeing the slaughter at a sacrifice, declares that non-violence is the highest dharma and that the killing of animals in sacrifice was introduced by the greedy, not taught by Manu.

title: Vijñānabhairava
summary: A dialogue in which the Goddess (Bhairavī) asks Bhairava about his true nature; he rejects every form 'with parts' (the ninefold, the mass of sounds, the three-headed, nāda-bindu...) as a device for the confused (vv. 7-13), describes the supreme state as indescribable fullness identical with the Goddess (14-21), and in answer to her request for means (22-23) teaches 112 contemplations (dhāraṇā) of the 'waveless state' (24-138; counted at 139). It then redefines japa, meditation, worship, oblation, sacrifice and bathing as inner acts (144-153), teaches the natural 'haṃsa' repetition of the breath (154-156), enjoins secrecy (157-160), and closes with the Goddess embracing Śiva, having grasped 'the essence of the Rudrayāmala' (161-163).

attribution.tradition: Spoken by Bhairava to Bhairavī; claims to be the essence of the Rudrayāmala and of the Trika (vv. 1, 161-162).
attribution.scholarly: Anonymous. The claimed Rudrayāmala origin cannot be verified: the early Rudrayāmala is lost, and the extant Rudrayāmala (Uttaratantra) is a different and later text. Cited by Kṣemarāja, who began a commentary on it.

tradition.text: Part of the revealed Rudrayāmala.

title: Yogabhāṣya (Vyāsa's commentary on the Yoga Sūtra)

attribution.tradition: By Vyāsa, identified with Veda-Vyāsa and with Bādarāyaṇa (Vijñānabhikṣu, Yogavārttika intro. and 1.1; Nārāyaṇatīrtha, Sūtrārthabodhinī intro.).
attribution.scholarly: The author's identity is unknown; Maas (following Bronkhorst and others) holds that sūtra and bhāṣya are one work by Patañjali; older scholarship placed the bhāṣya well after the sūtras. The bhāṣya cites 'Patañjali' by name once (3.44), a point used in this debate.

scholarly.text: c. 325–425 CE if one work with the sūtras (Maas); older estimates placed it later (6th–8th c.)

structure.description: running prose commentary on all 195 sūtras, headed by a maṅgala verse to the lord of serpents; each pāda closes 'iti śrīpātañjale sāṃkhyapravacane yogaśāstre ... vyāsabhāṣye'

summary: The oldest and authoritative commentary. It defines yoga as samādhi and names the five levels of mind (1.1); analyzes the vṛttis, the kleśas and their states (with a fifth, 'burnt-seed' state), karma and its fruition; gives the fourfold scheme modelled on medicine (2.15) and the sevenfold final insight (2.27); lists seated postures (2.46); explains saṃyama and the powers, the four kinds of yogin and the invitation of the celestials (3.51), and a detailed cosmology (3.26); and argues against Buddhist views of a momentary mind and of objects as mind-only (1.32, 4.14–24).

title: Yoga Sūtra of Patañjali

attribution.tradition: Composed by Patañjali as a re-teaching (anuśāsana, 1.1) of the yoga first taught by Hiraṇyagarbha (Vijñānabhikṣu, Rāmānanda Sarasvatī, Nāgeśa on 1.1); Patañjali is regarded as an incarnation of Śeṣa (Ananta), the lord of serpents, and identified with the grammarian of the Mahābhāṣya.
attribution.scholarly: Most scholars doubt that the Yoga author is the grammarian (c. 2nd c. BCE). Philipp A. Maas argues, following earlier arguments by J. Bronkhorst, that sūtras and bhāṣya form one work — the Pātañjala Yogaśāstra, as the colophons ('pātañjale sāṃkhyapravacane yogaśāstre') call it — by one author, c. 325–425 CE; others treat the sūtras as older than the bhāṣya.

tradition.text: not dated by the tradition (Patañjali as an incarnation of Śeṣa)

scholarly.text: c. 325–425 CE together with the bhāṣya (Maas); earlier proposals range from the 2nd c. BCE to the 5th c. CE

structure.description: 4 pādas: Samādhi (51 sūtras), Sādhana (55), Vibhūti (55), Kaivalya (34) = 195 sūtras in the Vyāsa-based vulgate (Ānandāśrama ed., and every local commentary e-text). Some editions count 196 by treating 'etena śabdādy antardhānam uktam' — part of the bhāṣya on 3.21 in the Ānandāśrama ed. — as a separate sūtra 3.22, shifting the later numbers of pāda 3 by one. This unit uses the 195-sūtra numbering.

summary: The root text of the Yoga darśana. It defines yoga as the stilling of the activities of the mind (1.2); teaches practice and dispassion, devotion to Īśvara and Oṃ, the obstacles and their remedies, the samāpattis and the kinds of samādhi (pāda 1); kriyā-yoga, the five afflictions, karma, the seer and the seen, and the first five of the eight limbs (pāda 2); concentration, meditation, samādhi, saṃyama, the transformations of mind and the powers with their warnings (pāda 3); and the sources of powers, karma and latent tendencies, the reality of objects, the non-self-luminosity of mind, the cloud of dharma and kaivalya (pāda 4).

attribution.tradition: Colophons ascribe it to Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, pupil of Govinda Bhagavatpāda.
attribution.scholarly: Disputed. P. Hacker and T. Leggett argued that it is an early work of the Advaita teacher Śaṅkara; T. S. Rukmani and others doubt the ascription and date it later; K. Harimoto critically edited the section on YS 1.23–28.

scholarly.text: uncertain: c. 8th c. CE if by Śaṅkara; later dates proposed

summary: A sub-commentary on Vyāsa's bhāṣya, first printed in 1952 (Madras Government Oriental Series), notable for its extended reasoning about Īśvara (1.23–28) and for the controversy over its ascription to Śaṅkara.

title: Yoga Vāsiṣṭha

attribution.tradition: composed by Vālmīki, author of the Rāmāyaṇa, and told to Bharadvāja: the dialogue in which Vasiṣṭha teaches Rāma, with Viśvāmitra present, at Daśaratha's court
attribution.scholarly: the vulgate is a Vedāntic revision of the Kashmiri Mokṣopāya (src:moksopaya), an anonymous 10th-c. philosophical poem; its non-dualism is close to but not identical with Śaṅkara's Advaita and shares vocabulary with Kashmiri Śaiva and Buddhist idealist thought

tradition.text: composed by Vālmīki; the teaching given by Vasiṣṭha to the young Rāma in the Tretā age

scholarly.text: the Kashmiri Mokṣopāya c. 10th c. CE (Slaje, c. 950); the Vedānta-oriented Yoga Vāsiṣṭha vulgate is a later revision (c. 11th-14th c.); older proposals ranged from the 6th to the 13th c.

structure.description: 6 prakaraṇas: Vairāgya (dispassion, 33 sargas), Mumukṣu-vyavahāra (conduct of the seeker, 20), Utpatti (origination, 122), Sthiti (persistence, 62), Upaśama (quiescence, 93), Nirvāṇa (liberation, pūrvārdha 128 + uttarārdha 216). The text names itself Mokṣopāya and claims 32,000 verses (2.17.6); the printed vulgate has roughly 27,000-29,000

summary: Vasiṣṭha teaches the despondent young Rāma that the world is a projection of mind within the one consciousness (cit), arising like a dream; that human effort (pauruṣa) guided by scripture and the good overrides fate, which is only past effort; that liberation comes by inquiry (vicāra) with the four gatekeepers (peace, inquiry, contentment, holy company), by the weakening of latent tendencies (vāsanā) and the stilling of mind and breath, through seven stages of knowledge to liberation while living. The teaching is carried by dozens of stories (Līlā, Karkaṭī, Lavaṇa, Śukra, Dāśūra, Prahlāda, Bali, Gādhi, Uddālaka, Suraghu, Vītahavya, Bhuśuṇḍa, Cūḍālā and Śikhidhvaja, the stone and others).

summary: A manual in ten paṭalas by Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya on yoga as the Dvaita tradition understands it: yoga is the supreme worship of Hari with devotion through prescribed action; one remembers Hari as the real agent within one's limbs; it describes the training of a devotee, study and reflection on Madhva's works, initiation by the ācārya, worship with mantra and nyāsa, contemplation of oneself as the reflection (pratibimba) of Nārāyaṇa in the heart, a graded list of disciplines crowned by hearing, reflection, meditation, samādhi and bhakti, and the presence of Hari in both the worshipper and the image.

summary: A commentary 'for the easy understanding of the slow-witted' by Bhāvāgaṇeśa, who says it condenses the meaning examined in the bhāṣya and 'by my teacher himself in the Vārttika' (Vijñānabhikṣu).

title: Yogasūtravṛtti of Nāgeśa (Nāgojī) Bhaṭṭa
summary: A vṛtti on the sūtras by the grammarian Nāgeśa Bhaṭṭa. On 1.1 it says the śāstra expounds in detail the yoga taught by Hiraṇyagarbha and others; on 1.2 it glosses citta as the inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and nirodha as a special, supersensible effort that dissolves the activities.
notes: Nāgeśa is reported to have written a longer and a shorter vṛtti (Bṛhatī, Laghvī) — which one the local raw_etexts file contains is not verified.

title: Yogatattva Upaniṣad

canon.group_scheme: editorial grouping of the 108 used by the Adyar Library series and most modern catalogues; the Muktikā itself lists the 108 by Veda only

attribution.tradition: Śruti: revealed, without human author (apauruṣeya); the Muktikā presents it as one of the 108 Upaniṣads that Rāma teaches Hanumān, each belonging to a Vedic śākhā
attribution.scholarly: anonymous; assigned to a Veda by the Muktikā list, not by any surviving śākhā transmission

tradition.text: Śruti: eternal and authorless; no human date

scholarly.text: Scholarly accounts differ by text. Several Yoga Upaniṣads (e.g. Amṛtabindu, Amṛtanāda, Kṣurikā, Tejobindu, Nādabindu, Dhyānabindu, Brahmavidyā, Yogatattva, Yogaśikhā, Haṃsa) survive in shorter northern versions that are older; the expanded southern recensions (as in this collection) borrow from medieval haṭha works and were probably compiled in South India, perhaps as late as the 18th c. (Bouy 1994).

summary: Viṣṇu teaches Brahmā: yoga and knowledge are both needed; four yogas (mantra, laya, haṭha, rāja) and four stages (ārambha, ghaṭa, paricaya, niṣpatti); eight-limbed haṭha with mudrās; diet, place, obstacles; signs and powers (to be hidden); the five element concentrations; praise of Oṃ.

editions.name: Īśādiviṃśottaraśatopaniṣadaḥ (Nirṇayasāgara collection of 120 Upaniṣads), South Indian recension carrying Upaniṣad Brahmayogin's opening maṅgala verses; e-text github.com/sanskrit/raw_etexts vedaH/misc/upaniShat/mixedPF/108_Upanishads.md
editions.licence: text public domain; e-text licence unstated

editions.name: Adyar Library Upaniṣad series (Schrader, Minor Upaniṣads vol. 1: Saṃnyāsa, 1912; A. Mahadeva Sastri: Yoga 1920, Sāmānya Vedānta 1921, Vaiṣṇava 1923, Śaiva 1925, Śākta 1925) with Upaniṣad Brahmayogin's commentary

notes: Refs follow the chapter/verse numbering of the Nirṇayasāgara-type e-text used here; other editions (e.g. the Adyar series, Schrader's critical edition, northern recensions) number differently.
key_teachings_note: 26 skeleton teachings in this shard; first 8 listed

title: Yogavallī
summary: A modern Sanskrit commentary on the Yoga Sūtras. Its introduction surveys the darśanas, gives the count of 195 sūtras (51, 55, 55, 34), notes that some manuscripts mark the end of the work after pāda 3, cites the verse from Bhoja's vṛtti on Patañjali's three kinds of purification, and compares the Vivaraṇa, Tattvavaiśāradī and Yogavārttika on particular sūtras.
notes: Only the Samādhipāda is in the local raw_etexts file; author and date not identified (gap).

title: Yogavārttika

scholarly.text: second half of the 16th c. CE

summary: Vijñānabhikṣu's extensive sub-commentary on the bhāṣya. It calls the bhāṣya 'the essence of all the Veda spoken by Vedavyāsa' and holds Sāṃkhya and the other darśanas to be contained in it like rivers in the ocean (intro.); cites the Yoga-Yājñavalkya for Hiraṇyagarbha as first teacher (1.1); argues for the mutual reflection of consciousness and buddhi against a single-reflection view (1.7); gives its own account of the four samprajñāta samādhis (1.17); and holds that knowledge of the Supreme Lord is the swift cause of liberation (1.51).

editions.name: ed. Jīvānanda Vidyāsāgara (Calcutta), with the bhāṣya; e-Bhāratī Sampat e-text

title: Yogaviṣaya
summary: A short tract of thirty-three verses attributed to Mīnanātha (Matsyendra): the qualified disciple, the six centres from ādhāra to ājñā, the three channels, the three knots of Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra, the names of kuṇḍalinī, the nectar raining from the brahma-place, inner worship with the flower of the mind, and the haṃsa repeated 21,600 times as 'so 'ham'.

editions.name: P. C. Bagchi (ed.), Kaulajñānanirṇaya and some minor texts of the school of Matsyendranātha, Calcutta Sanskrit Series 3 (Calcutta, 1934)
Muktabodha e-text M00121

notes: Colophon in the e-text reads 'matsyendranāthaviracitaṃ ...'; the text calls its author Mīnanātha, son of Umā and Śaṅkara (v. 7). Date uncertain.

summary: The book of the war: Vibhīṣaṇa's surrender and Rāma's vow to protect whoever seeks refuge, the war, Agastya's hymn to the Sun, Rāvaṇa's death, Sītā's ordeal, and the return to Ayodhyā.

attribution.tradition: the gopīs singing in pairs while Kṛṣṇa is away with the cows; recorded by Vyāsa in the Bhāgavata
attribution.scholarly: part of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa

tradition.text: composed by Vyāsa and recited by Śuka to Parīkṣit at the opening of the Kali age (traditional reckoning from 3102 BCE)

scholarly.text: c. 9th-10th c. CE (South India); some scholars allow earlier layers

summary: The gopīs' paired verses remembering Kṛṣṇa's pastimes during the day's separation.

title: Yugalaśataka
summary: Śrī Bhaṭṭa's hundred Braj Bhāṣā verses on the love-play of the divine couple (yugala) Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa; among the earliest Braj devotional texts.

title: Yūki vaittiya cintāmaṇi (Yūkimuṉi)
summary: A medical verse-treatise ascribed to Yūkimuṉi, much used for the classification of diseases by the humours.

title: Yuktidīpikā

attribution.tradition: A colophon in the edition names Vācaspati Miśra ('kṛtir iyaṃ śrīvācaspatimiśrāṇām').
attribution.scholarly: Anonymous; the colophon ascription to Vācaspati Miśra is not accepted.

structure.description: introductory verses and a commentary on the SK in four prakaraṇas and eleven āhnikas

summary: The most extensive old commentary on the SK. It defends Sāṃkhya against rival schools, preserves the divergent views of earlier Sāṃkhya teachers (Vārṣagaṇya, Vindhyavāsin, Pañcādhikaraṇa, Paurika, the Sāṃkhya teacher Patañjali), enumerates the sixty topics of the Ṣaṣṭitantra and gives a list of teachers between Pañcaśikha and Īśvarakṛṣṇa.

editions.name: Shiv Kumar & D. N. Bhargava (eds.), 2 vols., Delhi 1990–92; GRETIL/DCS e-text

title: Yuktimallikā

tradition.text: the tradition gives Vādirāja a life of 120 years (1480–1600)

summary: Vādirāja Tīrtha's major polemical verse treatise defending Dvaita doctrine — Viṣṇu's fullness of qualities, difference, the reality of the world and the nature of liberation — against Advaita.
notes: Its division into sections called 'saurabhas' is recalled at low confidence.

title: Yuktisnehaprapūraṇī
summary: Rāmakṛṣṇa Bhaṭṭa's commentary on the tarkapāda of the Śāstradīpikā (with the Siddhāntacandrikā).
